109\longrightarrow218.
\]
This is correct because the duplicated collection contains twice as much accumulated response time. The mean remains unchanged:
\[
\frac{218}{10}=21.8.
\]
Duplication changes the amount of data but not its average level. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}
&:\quad
\text{sensitive to how many contributions occur},\\
\text{mean}
&:\quad
\text{normalized by the number of contributions}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Two collections can have the same mean while having different totals:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10\\
20
\end{bmatrix}
\]
has mean
\[
15
\]
and total
\[
30,
\]
while
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10\\
20\\
10\\
20
\end{bmatrix}
\]
also has mean
\[
15
\]
but total
\[
60.
\]
The mean deliberately removes the effect of collection size from the accumulated magnitude.


2.3 Maximum: Preserve the Upper Extreme
The maximum asks:

Which value is at least as large as every value in the collection?

For the response times,
\[
\boxed{
M=\max_i x_i=31.
}
\]
Unlike the total, the maximum does not allow every value to contribute additively. A value affects the result only if it exceeds the current candidate. The maximum can also be composed across groups. For the groups
\[
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
B=
\begin{bmatrix}
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix},
\]
their maxima are
\[
\max(A)=25
\]
and
\[
\max(B)=31.
\]
The maximum of the complete collection is
\[
\max(25,31)=31.
\]
Thus,
\[
\max(A\cup B)
=
\max\bigl(\max(A),\max(B)\bigr).
\]
This compositional property makes maximum a reduction operator. Partial maxima can be combined to recover the global maximum. The maximum is associative:
\[
\max(\max(a,b),c)
=
\max(a,\max(b,c)).
\]
It is also idempotent:
\[
\max(x,x)=x.
\]
Repeating an existing value does not change the maximum. Duplicating the complete collection therefore leaves the result unchanged. This contrasts with total:
\[
x+x=2x,
\]
so duplication changes accumulated magnitude. The maximum preserves
\[
\boxed{
\text{the upper extreme of the collection}.
}
\]
It discards how many times that extreme occurs, how far other values lie below it, and how the values are distributed.


2.4 Minimum: Preserve the Lower Extreme
The minimum asks the complementary question:

Which value is no larger than every value in the collection?

For the response times,
\[
\boxed{
m=\min_i x_i=13.
}
\]
The required relationship is
\[
m\leq x_i
\qquad
\text{for every }i,
\]
and
\[
m=x_k
\qquad
\text{for at least one }k.
\]
Like maximum, minimum composes across groups:
\[
\min(A\cup B)
=
\min\bigl(\min(A),\min(B)\bigr).
\]
It is associative:
\[
\min(\min(a,b),c)
=
\min(a,\min(b,c)),
\]
and idempotent:
\[
\min(x,x)=x.
\]
Minimum preserves the lower extreme while discarding most other information. Maximum and minimum are related through negation:
\[
\min_i x_i
=
-\max_i(-x_i).
\]
To find the smallest original value, negate all values, find the largest negated value, and negate the result. For the collection,
\[
-\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-18\\
-25\\
-13\\
-31\\
-22
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The maximum of the negated values is
\[
-13.
\]
Negating it gives
\[
13,
\]
which is the original minimum. This equivalence shows that minimum and maximum express the same order structure viewed in opposite directions.


2.5 The Operators Preserve Different Facts
For the same collection,
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25\\
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix},
\]
the reductions produce:









Question
Reduction
Result
Property preserved




How much altogether?
\(\sum_i x_i\)
\(109\)
accumulated magnitude


What equal-share level?
\(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\)
\(21.8\)
average level


What upper extreme?
\(\max_i x_i\)
\(31\)
largest value


What lower extreme?
\(\min_i x_i\)
\(13\)
smallest value



The results cannot be substituted for one another. A maximum of \(31\) does not reveal a total of \(109\). A mean of \(21.8\) does not reveal a minimum of \(13\). Each scalar is correct only relative to the question it was designed to answer. This is why choosing a reduction is a semantic decision before it is a programming decision.


2.6 Similar Results Do Not Imply Equivalent Reductions
For a single-value collection
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
7
\end{bmatrix},
\]
we obtain
\[
\sum_i x_i=7,
\]
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i=7,
\]
\[
\max_i x_i=7,
\]
and
\[
\min_i x_i=7.
\]
All four reductions produce the same number. Nevertheless, they do not have the same meaning. Their differences appear when the input changes. For
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
7\\
5
\end{bmatrix},
\]
the results are
\[
\text{total}=12,
\]
\[
\text{mean}=6,
\]
\[
\text{maximum}=7,
\]
and
\[
\text{minimum}=5.
\]
Agreement on one special input does not establish equivalence between functions. Two reductions are equivalent only if they produce the same result for every admissible input in the domain. This principle prevents a common reasoning error: identifying a mathematical operation only from one numerical example. Meaning comes from the relationship the operator defines across its domain.


2.7 Units Help Distinguish the Questions
Each response time \(x_i\) is measured in milliseconds. The maximum and minimum are also measured in milliseconds:
\[
\max_i x_i=31\text{ ms},
\]
\[
\min_i x_i=13\text{ ms}.
\]
The mean is measured in milliseconds per observation, which is ordinarily reported as milliseconds because each observation is one request:
\[
\bar{x}=21.8\text{ ms per request}.
\]
The interpretation of the total requires greater care. If the values represent durations of separate requests and the question asks for accumulated duration, then
\[
\sum_i x_i=109\text{ ms}
\]
is meaningful as the sum of those durations. It does not necessarily mean that \(109\) milliseconds elapsed on a wall clock. If requests occurred concurrently, their accumulated durations and elapsed time would be different quantities.This illustrates that algebraic compatibility is not sufficient for semantic validity. Quantities may share units and still answer different real-world questions.
Before reducing, the reader should ask:

What does combining these quantities mean in the model of the problem?



2.8 Partial Results and the Information Needed to Combine Them
Suppose a large collection is divided into several parts. A useful reduction often allows partial results to be combined. For totals, store one partial sum per group:
\[
T_A=\sum_{i\in A}x_i,
\]
\[
T_B=\sum_{i\in B}x_i.
\]
Then
\[
T=T_A+T_B.
\]
For maximum,
\[
M=\max(M_A,M_B).
\]
For minimum,
\[
m=\min(m_A,m_B).
\]
The mean requires more information. The means of two groups cannot generally be averaged directly unless the groups have equal sizes. Suppose group \(A\) has mean \(\bar{x}_A\) and size \(n_A\), while group \(B\) has mean \(\bar{x}_B\) and size \(n_B\). Their combined mean is
\[
\boxed{
\bar{x}
=
\frac{n_A\bar{x}_A+n_B\bar{x}_B}{n_A+n_B}.
}
\]
The group sizes are needed because each mean represents a different number of observations. Equivalently, each group can preserve its total and count:
\[
(T_A,n_A),
\qquad
(T_B,n_B).
\]
The combined mean is then
\[
\bar{x}
=
\frac{T_A+T_B}{n_A+n_B}.
\]
This reveals that a mean is not compositionally complete as one scalar unless group sizes are also known. Different reductions require different sufficient information for later combination.


2.9 The Question Determines the Algebra
The words used in a problem suggest different invariants:

“altogether” asks for accumulated magnitude;
“per observation” asks for normalized magnitude;
“largest” asks for an upper bound attained by the data;
“smallest” asks for a lower bound attained by the data.

These meanings determine the mathematical operator:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{total}
&\longrightarrow
\sum_i x_i,\\
\text{mean}
&\longrightarrow
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i,\\
\text{upper extreme}
&\longrightarrow
\max_i x_i,\\
\text{lower extreme}
&\longrightarrow
\min_i x_i.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The correct reasoning order is
\[
\boxed{
\text{global question}
\rightarrow
\text{property to preserve}
\rightarrow
\text{combination rule}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced value}.
}
\]
The unsafe order is to select a familiar library function first and then invent a meaning for its result. All four reductions return values. A different kind of question remains unanswered:

At which position does an extreme occur?

The largest value and the location of that value are distinct mathematical objects. The next section will construct this distinction through maximum and argmax.

title: Chapter 10 — Dimension Reduction
section: 3 10.3 The Reduced Value and Its Location Are Different Objects
text:
3 10.3 The Reduced Value and Its Location Are Different Objects
Consider again the response times
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25\\
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Section 10.2 asked:

What is the largest response time?

The answer is
\[
\max_i x_i=31.
\]
Now consider a different question:

At which position did the largest response time occur?

The answer is
\[
4.
\]
The numbers \(31\) and \(4\) are related, but they do not represent the same kind of object. The number \(31\) is a response-time value. The number \(4\) is an index identifying a position in the collection. The relationship between them is
\[
x_4=31.
\]
Maximum returns the value:
\[
\boxed{
\max_i x_i=31.
}
\]
Argmax returns the location:
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=4.
}
\]
The name argmax is an abbreviation for “argument of the maximum.” Here, the argument is the index \(i\) supplied to the indexed collection \(x_i\). Argmax returns the index at which the largest value is attained.

3.1 Value Space and Index Space
The response-time values belong to a numerical measurement space. In this example,
\[
x_i\in\mathbb{R},
\]
with each value interpreted in milliseconds. The indices belong to the index set
\[
\mathcal{I}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\max_i x_i\in\mathbb{R},
\]
while
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i\in\mathcal{I}
\]
when the maximum occurs at exactly one position. The two reductions have different codomains:
\[
\max:\mathbb{R}^{5}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
\]
whereas
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}:\mathbb{R}^{5}\rightarrow\mathcal{I}.
\]
Maximum returns an element of the value space. Argmax returns an element of the position space. This distinction is semantic, not merely notational. The result
\[
31
\]
means “31 milliseconds.” The result
\[
4
\]
means “the fourth position.” Treating the index \(4\) as though it were a response time would confuse a location with the value stored there.


3.2 Argmax Is Defined Through Maximum
Let
\[
M=\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_i.
\]
The argmax is the set of indices whose values equal \(M\):
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_i
=
\{i\in\mathcal{I}:x_i=M\}.
}
\]
For the concrete collection,
\[
M=31.
\]
We inspect the indexed values:
\[
x_1=18\neq31,
\]
\[
x_2=25\neq31,
\]
\[
x_3=13\neq31,
\]
\[
x_4=31,
\]
and
\[
x_5=22\neq31.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_i
=
\{4\}.
\]
When the maximizing index is unique, mathematical writing often simplifies the singleton set and writes
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=4.
\]
More precisely, the argmax is the set \(\{4\}\), while \(4\) is its unique member.
The defining relationship is
\[
\boxed{
i^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_{i^\star}=\max_i x_i.
}
\]
The symbol \(i^\star\) denotes a maximizing index. Once the location \(i^\star\) has been found, indexing the collection at that location recovers the maximum value:
\[
x_{i^\star}=M.
\]
For the response times,
\[
i^\star=4
\]
and
\[
x_{i^\star}=x_4=31.
\]


3.3 Maximum Does Not Reveal Argmax
Knowing only that
\[
\max_i x_i=31
\]
does not determine where \(31\) occurs. Consider
\[
\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
31\\
18\\
25
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{b}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25\\
31
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Both collections have the same maximum:
\[
\max_i a_i=31,
\]
\[
\max_i b_i=31.
\]
But their maximizing positions differ:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i a_i=1,
\]
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i b_i=3.
\]
The maximum preserves the upper extreme while discarding its location. Once the collection has been reduced to the scalar \(31\), the positional information cannot be reconstructed. Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{maximum value alone does not determine its location}.
}
\]


3.4 Argmax Does Not Reveal Maximum
The reverse is also true. Knowing only that
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=4
\]
does not determine the largest value. The collections
\[
\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
2\\
3\\
10\\
4
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{b}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25\\
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix}
\]
both satisfy
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i a_i=4
\]
and
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i b_i=4.
\]
However,
\[
\max_i a_i=10,
\]
while
\[
\max_i b_i=31.
\]
Argmax preserves the location of the upper extreme while discarding its magnitude. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\text{location alone does not determine the value located there}.
}
\]
To preserve both pieces of information, the computation must retain the pair
\[
(i^\star,x_{i^\star}).
\]
For the response-time example, this pair is
\[
(4,31).
\]
The first component identifies where the event occurred. The second identifies its measured magnitude.


3.5 Units Expose the Difference
Each response time has units of milliseconds:
\[
x_i\text{ is measured in milliseconds}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\max_i x_i=31\text{ ms}.
\]
The argmax has no unit of milliseconds:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=4.
\]
The index \(4\) is a positional label. Depending on the problem, it might refer to:

the fourth request;
the fourth class;
the fourth time step;
the fourth pixel;
the fourth candidate;
the fourth row of a matrix.

The index acquires meaning from the index domain, not from the units of the values.


3.6 A Search Variable and an Objective Value
Argmax notation becomes especially meaningful when written as an optimization problem. Suppose a function
\[
f(i)
\]
assigns a value to every candidate index \(i\in\mathcal{I}\).The maximum objective value is
\[
\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}}f(i).
\]
A maximizing argument is
\[
i^\star
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}f(i).
\]
These answer two different questions:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}}f(i)
&:\quad
\text{How large can the objective become?}\\
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}f(i)
&:\quad
\text{Which candidate makes it that large?}
\end{aligned}
}
\]
For an indexed vector, the objective function is
\[
f(i)=x_i.
\]
The search variable is \(i\), not \(x_i\). This explains the word argument: argmax returns the input to the function that produces the largest output. The distinction appears throughout mathematical programming. A classification model may produce one score per class:
\[
s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_k.
\]
The maximum score answers
\[
\max_j s_j,
\]
while the predicted class is often
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_j s_j.
\]
The score and class label are different objects even when both are represented numerically.


3.7 Ties Make Argmax Set-Valued
Now consider
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
31\\
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The maximum remains
\[
\max_i x_i=31.
\]
However, the value \(31\) occurs at positions \(2\) and \(4\). Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=\{2,4\}.
}
\]
This reveals an important mathematical fact: argmax is naturally set-valued. It returns all arguments at which the maximum is attained. When the maximum is unique, the set contains one element:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=\{4\}.
\]
When the maximum is tied, the set contains several elements:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=\{2,4\}.
\]
A programming library often returns only one index. For example, it may return the first maximizing position:
response_times = [18, 31, 13, 31, 22]
largest_position = response_times.index(max(response_times))
Using zero-based Python indexing, this returns
1
because the first occurrence of \(31\) is at Python index 1.This behavior includes a tie-breaking rule:

If several positions attain the maximum, return the first one under the library’s indexing order.

That is a valid software contract, but it is more specific than the mathematical argmax set. The program has chosen one representative from
\[
\{2,4\}
\]
under one-based mathematical indexing, or from
\[
\{1,3\}
\]
under zero-based Python indexing. The tie-breaking policy should not be mistaken for a mathematical proof that the maximizer is unique.


3.8 Indexing Conventions Change the Numerical Label
Mathematical exposition commonly labels positions as
\[
1,2,\ldots,n.
\]
Python labels the same positions as
\[
0,1,\ldots,n-1.
\]
For
response_times = [18, 25, 13, 31, 22]
the mathematical position of \(31\) is
\[
4,
\]
but its Python index is
3
because Python begins indexing at zero. Thus,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\{1,\ldots,5\}}x_i=4
\]
and a Python argmax operation may return
3
without disagreement. The two results use different coordinate conventions. An index has meaning only relative to an explicitly understood index system. The safe translation is
\[
\boxed{
\text{mathematical position }i
=
\text{Python index }i-1.
}
\]
This offset applies only when the mathematical convention begins at \(1\) and the programming convention begins at \(0\).


3.9 Reordering Preserves Maximum but Changes Argmax
Consider the original collection
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
25\\
13\\
31\\
22
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its maximum and argmax are
\[
\max_i x_i=31
\]
and
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i=4.
\]
Now rearrange the values:
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
31\\
18\\
22\\
25\\
13
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The maximum remains
\[
\max_i\widetilde{x}_i=31.
\]
The argmax becomes
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i\widetilde{x}_i=1.
\]
Maximum is invariant under reordering because the upper extreme does not depend on where the values are placed. Argmax is not invariant because it reports a location. Instead, argmax follows the permutation. If the maximizing value moves from position \(4\) to position \(1\), its maximizing index moves correspondingly. Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{maximum}
&:\quad
\text{preserves value under reordering},\\
\text{argmax}
&:\quad
\text{tracks the reordered location}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


3.10 Minimum and Argmin Have the Same Distinction
The smallest response time is
\[
\min_i x_i=13.
\]
Its location is
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_i x_i=3
\]
under one-based indexing. Minimum returns a value:
\[
\min_i x_i\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Argmin returns an index or set of indices:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_i x_i\subseteq\mathcal{I}.
\]
Formally,
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_i
=
\left\{
i\in\mathcal{I}:
x_i=\min_{j\in\mathcal{I}}x_j
\right\}.
}
\]
The same questions arise:

Is the minimizing position unique?
Which indexing convention is used?
If several minima occur, which tie-breaking rule does the software apply?
Does the computation need the value, the position, or both?



3.11 The Structural Difference
Maximum and argmax both inspect the entire indexed collection, but they preserve different aspects of it:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\max_i x_i
&:\quad
\text{preserves the extreme value and discards its position},\\
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i
&:\quad
\text{preserves the extreme position and discards its value}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Retaining both requires
\[
\boxed{
\left(
i^\star,
x_{i^\star}
\right),
\qquad
i^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i x_i.
}
\]
This distinction becomes even more important for matrices and tensors, where a reduction may eliminate one index while preserving others. The next section will examine how reducing along a chosen axis determines which indices disappear and which remain in the output.

title: Chapter 10 — Dimension Reduction
section: 4 10.4 Reducing One Axis While Preserving Another
text:
4 10.4 Reducing One Axis While Preserving Another
A vector has one index:
\[
x_i.
\]
Reducing that index produces a scalar:
\[
r=\max_i x_i.
\]
The index \(i\) appears inside the reduction operator but does not appear on the result. We described this by saying that the reduction consumes or eliminates the index. A matrix has two indices:
\[
X_{ij}.
\]
The first index \(i\) identifies a row, and the second index \(j\) identifies a column. A reduction may eliminate both indices, producing one scalar, or eliminate only one index, producing a vector indexed by the dimension that remains. This leads to a general principle:
\[
\boxed{
\text{a reduced index disappears from the output;
an unreduced index remains}.
}
\]

4.1 A Matrix with Two Kinds of Position
Suppose three computer servers handle four requests. Their response times, measured in milliseconds, are
\[
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18 & 25 & 13 & 31\\
22 & 20 & 24 & 19\\
35 & 28 & 30 & 26
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Let the row index
\[
i\in\{1,2,3\}
\]
identify the server, and let the column index
\[
j\in\{1,2,3,4\}
\]
identify the request. Thus,
\[
X_{ij}
=
\text{response time of server }i
\text{ for request }j.
\]
For example,
\[
X_{2,3}=24
\]
means that server \(2\) took \(24\) milliseconds to handle request \(3\). The matrix belongs to
\[
\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}.
\]
The shape \((3,4)\) records that the matrix contains three server positions and four request positions. The semantic interpretation of those dimensions is
\[
(\text{servers},\text{requests}).
\]
The shape alone does not contain these names. They come from the model of the problem.


4.2 One Maximum for Each Server
Suppose we ask:

What was the largest response time produced by each server?

For server \(1\), the relevant values are
\[
18,\quad25,\quad13,\quad31,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
31.
\]
For server \(2\),
\[
22,\quad20,\quad24,\quad19,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
24.
\]
For server \(3\),
\[
35,\quad28,\quad30,\quad26,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
35.
\]
The result is the vector
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
31\\
24\\
35
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
There is one output for every server. Therefore the server index \(i\) remains:
\[
y_i.
\]
The request index \(j\) is reduced because all request values associated with one server are combined into one maximum:
\[
\boxed{
y_i=\max_{1\leq j\leq4}X_{ij}.
}
\]
The index structure makes the operation explicit:

\(i\) remains free and identifies the output component;
\(j\) is bound by the maximum and disappears from the output.

For each fixed \(i\), the maximum ranges over every admissible \(j\).
The shape transformation is
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}^{3}.
}
\]
The request dimension has been removed, while the server dimension has been preserved.


4.3 Fix One Index and Reduce the Other
The expression
\[
y_i=\max_j X_{ij}
\]
can be read as a two-stage instruction. First, fix a server index \(i\). For example, choose \(i=2\). This selects the row
\[
X_{2,1},X_{2,2},X_{2,3},X_{2,4}.
\]
Second, reduce across the request index \(j\):
\[
y_2
=
\max
\left(
X_{2,1},
X_{2,2},
X_{2,3},
X_{2,4}
\right).
\]
Substituting the values gives
\[
y_2=\max(22,20,24,19)=24.
\]
Repeating this relationship for every fixed \(i\) constructs the output vector. This is not one global maximum over the whole matrix. It is a family of reductions: one reduction for every value of the preserved index. The distinction is
\[
\boxed{
\text{fix the index that remains;
range over the index being reduced}.
}
\]


4.4 One Maximum for Each Request
Now ask a different question:

What was the largest response time observed for each request across all servers?

For request \(1\), the server values are
\[
18,\quad22,\quad35,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
35.
\]
For request \(2\),
\[
25,\quad20,\quad28,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
28.
\]
For request \(3\),
\[
13,\quad24,\quad30,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
30.
\]
For request \(4\),
\[
31,\quad19,\quad26,
\]
so the maximum is
\[
31.
\]
The output is
\[
\mathbf{z}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
35\\
28\\
30\\
31
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
There is one result for each request. Therefore the request index \(j\) remains:
\[
z_j.
\]
The server index \(i\) is reduced:
\[
\boxed{
z_j=\max_{1\leq i\leq3}X_{ij}.
}
\]
The shape transformation is
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}^{4}.
}
\]
This time the server dimension disappears and the request dimension remains.


4.5 Similar Operators Can Answer Different Questions
The expressions
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}
\]
and
\[
z_j=\max_iX_{ij}
\]
use the same maximum operator. They do not perform the same reduction. The first means:

For each server \(i\), find the maximum over requests \(j\).

The second means:

For each request \(j\), find the maximum over servers \(i\).

Their outputs have different lengths:
\[
\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},
\]
\[
\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}.
\]
They also have different semantic meanings. The components of \(\mathbf{y}\) describe servers. The components of \(\mathbf{z}\) describe requests. The choice of reduced axis is therefore part of the mathematical question, not merely a parameter supplied to a library function.


4.6 Reducing Both Indices
Suppose we ask:

What was the largest response time anywhere in the matrix?

Now neither a server-specific nor a request-specific index should remain. The complete reduction is
\[
r=\max_{i,j}X_{ij}.
\]
For the concrete matrix,
\[
r=35.
\]
Both indices are consumed by the reduction, so the output is a scalar:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}.
}
\]
The three possibilities can be compared:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}
&:\quad
\text{preserve }i,\text{ reduce }j,\\
z_j=\max_iX_{ij}
&:\quad
\text{reduce }i,\text{ preserve }j,\\
r=\max_{i,j}X_{ij}
&:\quad
\text{reduce both }i\text{ and }j.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The indices present on the left side reveal the shape of the output.


4.7 The Same Axis Logic Applies to Other Reductions
The distinction is not specific to maximum. The total response time for each server is
\[
T_i=\sum_{j=1}^{4}X_{ij}.
\]
For the concrete matrix,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_1&=18+25+13+31=87,\\
T_2&=22+20+24+19=85,\\
T_3&=35+28+30+26=119.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbf{T}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
87\\
85\\
119
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The request index \(j\) has been reduced, while the server index \(i\) remains. The average response time for each server is
\[
\bar{X}_i
=
\frac{1}{4}
\sum_{j=1}^{4}X_{ij}.
\]
The results are
\[
\bar{X}_1=21.75,
\]
\[
\bar{X}_2=21.25,
\]
and
\[
\bar{X}_3=29.75.
\]
Again, there is one result per server. The minimum response time for each request is
\[
m_j=\min_iX_{ij}.
\]
This reduces the server index \(i\) and preserves the request index \(j\). The reduction operator determines what property is preserved. The chosen axis determines which kind of position remains represented in the output.


4.8 Axis Means an Index Direction
In array programming, the word axis refers to one dimension of an array’s index structure.
For
\[
X_{ij},
\]
the first axis corresponds to \(i\), and the second axis corresponds to \(j\). Under the current interpretation,
\[
i=\text{server index},
\]
\[
j=\text{request index}.
\]
To reduce along an axis means to range over that axis’s index and eliminate it from the output. This language can be confusing because people sometimes say “calculate the row maximum” when they mean either:

find a maximum within every row;
reduce the row dimension.

These are not the same instruction. Finding a maximum within every row means ranging across columns:
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}.
\]
The row index remains. Reducing the row axis means ranging across rows:
\[
z_j=\max_iX_{ij}.
\]
The row index disappears. The safest wording is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{reduce over the index that should disappear}.
}
\]


4.9 Translating the Axes into NumPy
Represent the matrix in Python:
import numpy as np

response_times = np.array([
    [18, 25, 13, 31],
    [22, 20, 24, 19],
    [35, 28, 30, 26],
])
Its shape is
(3, 4)
NumPy calls the first dimension axis=0 and the second dimension axis=1. Reducing with
response_times.max(axis=1)
eliminates the second dimension. The operation ranges across columns within each row and returns one value per row:
[31, 24, 35]
Mathematically,
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}.
\]
Reducing with
response_times.max(axis=0)
eliminates the first dimension. The operation ranges across rows and returns one value per column:
[35, 28, 30, 31]
Mathematically,
\[
z_j=\max_iX_{ij}.
\]
Reducing without specifying an axis,
response_times.max()
reduces the entire array and returns
35
Mathematically,
\[
r=\max_{i,j}X_{ij}.
\]
The numerical axis parameter identifies the dimension to remove:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{axis=0}
&:\quad
\text{remove the first index},\\
\texttt{axis=1}
&:\quad
\text{remove the second index}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The parameter does not describe the meaning of the dimension. NumPy does not know that axis \(0\) represents servers or that axis \(1\) represents requests. The programmer must preserve that semantic interpretation.
Suppose the same numerical matrix is stored with the opposite orientation:
\[
\widetilde{X}_{ji}
=
\text{response time for request }j
\text{ on server }i.
\]
Its shape would be
\[
(4,3)
\]
rather than
\[
(3,4).
\]
Now the request index is first and the server index is second. A per-server reduction would use a different numerical axis than before. This demonstrates that axis=0 does not inherently mean “server” or “sample,” and axis=1 does not inherently mean “request” or “feature.” Axis numbers refer to storage positions in the shape tuple. Their semantic meanings depend on how the data was organized. The correct reasoning order is
\[
\boxed{
\text{question}
\rightarrow
\text{index to preserve}
\rightarrow
\text{index to reduce}
\rightarrow
\text{numerical axis}.
}
\]
Choosing an axis merely because a familiar example used the same number can produce a mechanically valid result with the wrong meaning.


4.10 Preserving a Reduced Dimension as Size One
Some numerical libraries allow a reduced dimension to remain in the output with length \(1\).
For example,
response_times.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
produces an array with shape
(3, 1)
rather than
(3,)
and values
[[31],
 [24],
 [35]]
The reduction still ranges over the request index \(j\). There is still only one maximum per server. The singleton dimension is retained as a structural placeholder. Without preservation,
\[
\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}^{3}.
\]
With a singleton dimension retained,
\[
\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}^{3\times1}.
\]
The reduced index no longer varies over four request positions. It has been collapsed to one summary position. Retaining a size-one dimension can help later operations align shapes, but it does not restore the information removed by the reduction. The four original request values cannot be recovered from one maximum. Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{keeping the dimension is not the same as keeping the data}.
}
\]


4.11 Argmax Along an Axis
The distinction between value and location also applies to axis reductions. For each server, the largest response time is
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}.
\]
The request position at which that maximum occurs is
\[
q_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_jX_{ij}.
\]
For the concrete matrix,
\[
\mathbf{q}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4\\
3\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
under one-based indexing:

server \(1\) has its maximum at request \(4\);
server \(2\) has its maximum at request \(3\);
server \(3\) has its maximum at request \(1\).

The output retains the server index \(i\) because there is one maximizing request position for each server:
\[
q_i.
\]
The reduced request index \(j\) reappears as the value stored in \(q_i\). This does not mean that \(j\) remains as an output dimension. Instead, a selected value from the request index set becomes the content of each output component. The value and location outputs are
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij}
\]
and
\[
q_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_jX_{ij}.
\]
Their relationship is
\[
X_{i,q_i}=y_i.
\]


4.12 Generalizing to More Dimensions
Suppose a tensor has components
\[
X_{ijk}.
\]
A reduction over \(k\) produces
\[
Y_{ij}=\sum_kX_{ijk}.
\]
The index \(k\) disappears, while \(i\) and \(j\) remain. A reduction over \(j\) and \(k\) produces
\[
Z_i=\max_{j,k}X_{ijk}.
\]
Only \(i\) remains. A complete reduction produces
\[
r=\min_{i,j,k}X_{ijk}.
\]
No index remains. The general rule is visible directly from the notation:
\[
\boxed{
\text{indices on the right but not the left are reduced}.
}
\]
This provides a mathematical method for predicting output shape before writing code. If
\[
X_{i_1i_2\ldots i_d}
\]
has \(d\) indices and a reduction eliminates a subset of them, the output retains exactly the complementary subset of indices.


4.13 Reduction as a Transformation of Index Structure
An axis reduction does two things simultaneously:

it combines numerical values according to an operator;
it transforms the index structure of the object.

For
\[
y_i=\max_jX_{ij},
\]
the maximum operator preserves the upper extreme across \(j\), while the index transformation removes the request dimension and preserves the server dimension. The numerical and structural questions are distinct:

Which property should be preserved across the reduced positions?

and

Which positions should remain represented in the output?

The first determines whether we use sum, mean, maximum, minimum, or another reduction. The second determines the axis. The complete design process is
\[
\boxed{
\text{global question}
\rightarrow
\text{reduction operator}
\rightarrow
\text{index to eliminate}
\rightarrow
\text{output index structure}.
}
\]
For the server matrix:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{largest time per server}
&\rightarrow
\max
\rightarrow
\text{eliminate request index }j
\rightarrow
y_i,\\
\text{largest time per request}
&\rightarrow
\max
\rightarrow
\text{eliminate server index }i
\rightarrow
z_j,\\
\text{largest time overall}
&\rightarrow
\max
\rightarrow
\text{eliminate }i\text{ and }j
\rightarrow
r.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
A reduction is therefore not adequately described by saying that “many values become one.” In multidimensional data, many values may become one value for every remaining index. The more precise principle is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{many values along the reduced indices
become one value for each configuration of the preserved indices}.
}
\]
The chapter has now established how reductions choose a property, return a value or location, and transform index structure. The final section will examine reduction as deliberate information loss: what the reduced result preserves, what it destroys, and why that loss is necessary for the summary to perform its intended role.

title: Chapter 10 — Dimension Reduction
section: 5 10.5 Reduction as Deliberate Information Loss
text:
5 10.5 Reduction as Deliberate Information Loss
A computation need not retain only one reduced value. It can preserve several summaries:
\[
S(\mathbf{x})
=
\left(
\min_i x_i,
\max_i x_i,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i
\right).
\]
For the response times,
\[
S(\mathbf{x})
=
(13,31,21.8).
\]
This summary distinguishes more collections than any one of its components alone. Two vectors with the same mean but different maxima no longer produce the same combined summary. However, even the triple
\[
(\text{minimum},\text{maximum},\text{mean})
\]
does not generally reconstruct the original data. For example,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
2\\
4
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
1\\
5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
do not have the same maximum, so they are distinguished. But other distinct collections can share the same minimum, maximum, and mean. For instance,
\[
\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
2\\
4\\
6
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{b}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
3\\
3\\
6
\end{bmatrix}
\]
both have
\[
\min=0,
\]
\[
\max=6,
\]
and
\[
\text{mean}=3.
\]
Yet
\[
\mathbf{a}\neq\mathbf{b}.
\]
Adding summaries can preserve more properties without preserving the complete input. This creates a spectrum:
\[
\boxed{
\text{less summary information}
\longrightarrow
\text{more indistinguishable inputs}
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\text{more summary information}
\longrightarrow
\text{fewer indistinguishable inputs}.
}
\]
The appropriate point on this spectrum depends on the task, storage constraints, computational needs, and future questions.
Suppose we preserve both the total
\[
T=\sum_i x_i
\]
and the count
\[
n.
\]
The mean can be reconstructed:
\[
\bar{x}=\frac{T}{n}.
\]
Therefore, the pair
\[
(T,n)
\]
contains enough information to compute the mean. The mean alone does not generally contain enough information to recover the total because the count may be unknown. A mean of \(10\) could come from
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10
\end{bmatrix},
\]
with total \(10\), or
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
10\\
10\\
10
\end{bmatrix},
\]
with total \(30\). This establishes an ordering of information content. If one summary can be computed from another, the second summary preserves at least enough information for the first. Symbolically, if
\[
R_2(\mathbf{x})=h(R_1(\mathbf{x}))
\]
for some function \(h\), then \(R_1\) contains sufficient information to derive \(R_2\). For example,
\[
\text{mean}
=
h(\text{total},\text{count})
\]
with
\[
h(T,n)=\frac{T}{n}.
\]
But total and count cannot generally be reconstructed from mean alone. The direction of derivability reveals which summary is more informative for a specified family of questions.

5.1 Reduction Can Remove Meaningful Context
Suppose response times are ordered chronologically:
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n.
\]
The maximum preserves the worst observed duration but removes when it occurred. The mean preserves average level but removes temporal patterns. Two systems could have the same mean while one steadily degrades and the other remains stable. Similarly, reducing an image to its average brightness removes spatial arrangement. Two images with the same average may depict entirely different scenes. The lost context may be irrelevant to the immediate decision and essential to later analysis. A reduction should therefore be treated as a commitment:
\[
\boxed{
\text{after reduction, only properties encoded in the result remain available}.
}
\]


5.2 Choosing a Reduction Is Choosing an Invariant
A mathematical invariant is a property that remains unchanged under some transformations or variations. The sum is invariant under any rearrangement or redistribution that preserves total magnitude. The mean is invariant under changes that preserve both total relative to count. The maximum is invariant under changes to nonmaximal values that remain below the maximum. Argmax is invariant under changes that do not alter which index attains the maximum. Each reduction declares certain distinctions irrelevant. For maximum,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
31\\
1\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
31\\
30\\
29
\end{bmatrix}
\]
are equivalent because both preserve the upper extreme \(31\). For sum, they are different because their totals differ. The reduction operator therefore encodes a philosophy of relevance:

Preserve this property; ignore distinctions that do not affect it.

This is why reduction belongs to problem formulation rather than merely implementation.


5.3 A Responsible Reduction Workflow
Before reducing a collection, determine the global question:

What must the output tell us?

Then identify the property that answers that question:
\[
\text{total},
\quad
\text{average},
\quad
\text{extreme value},
\quad
\text{extreme location},
\quad
\text{or another summary}.
\]
Next, determine which indices may be eliminated and which must remain. If the output must retain one result per server, preserve the server index. If it must retain one result per class, preserve the class index. Then ask what future questions will be impossible after the reduction. This does not require preserving every possible detail, but it makes the loss explicit.

title: Chapter 6 — Selective Updates
text:
Consider five temperature readings produced by a sensor:
readings = [18, 24, 16, 27, 19]
A calibration test has established that readings below \(20\) degrees Celsius under-report the actual temperature by \(2\) degrees. Such readings must therefore be increased by \(2\), while readings of at least \(20\) degrees must remain unchanged. An ordinary program can express this requirement through a branch inside a loop:
readings = [18, 24, 16, 27, 19]
corrected_readings = []

for reading in readings:
    if reading < 20:
        corrected_readings.append(reading + 2)
    else:
        corrected_readings.append(reading)
The resulting collection is
[20, 24, 18, 27, 21]
This computation begins with one collection and constructs another:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
24\\
16\\
27\\
19
\end{bmatrix}
\longrightarrow
\begin{bmatrix}
20\\
24\\
18\\
27\\
21
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The condition does not determine whether a value should exist in the output. Every sensor position remains present. Instead, the condition determines whether the value at that position should change. This is the central distinction between masking and selective updating. In Chapter 5, masking answered:

Should the numerical contribution at this position survive or be suppressed to zero?

The present computation asks:

Should the value at this position be changed or preserved?

Suppression and preservation are not interchangeable. If a reading does not require correction, the required result is not zero. The required result is the original reading itself.


To represent change mathematically, we must distinguish the value before the update from the value after the update. Let
\[
x_i
\]
denote the original reading at position \(i\), and let
\[
x_i'
\]
denote the corrected reading at the same position. The prime symbol in \(x_i'\) does not mean differentiation here. It labels a new version of the quantity. Both \(x_i\) and \(x_i'\) refer to the same sensor position, but they refer to different states of its value:
\[
x_i
=
\text{value before correction},
\]
\[
x_i'
=
\text{value after correction}.
\]
This notation prevents a conceptual ambiguity that ordinary assignment syntax can hide. In code such as
reading = reading + 2
the name reading appears on both sides. On the right, it refers to the old value; after assignment, the same name refers to the new value. Mathematics makes the two roles explicit:
\[
\text{old state}
\longrightarrow
\text{new state}.
\]
For the five readings, the corresponding state pairs are
\[
x_1=18
\longrightarrow
x_1'=20,
\]
\[
x_2=24
\longrightarrow
x_2'=24,
\]
\[
x_3=16
\longrightarrow
x_3'=18,
\]
\[
x_4=27
\longrightarrow
x_4'=27,
\]
and
\[
x_5=19
\longrightarrow
x_5'=21.
\]
Some positions undergo a numerical change, while others satisfy
\[
x_i'=x_i.
\]
This equality expresses preservation. It says that the transition from the original state to the updated state leaves the value invariant.



Before searching for one algebraic expression, write the required update as a piecewise relationship:
\[
x_i'
=
\begin{cases}
x_i+2, & x_i<20,\\
x_i, & x_i\geq20.
\end{cases}
\]
This relationship contains two different state transitions. For a reading below \(20\), the transition is
\[
x_i\longrightarrow x_i+2.
\]
For a reading of at least \(20\), the transition is
\[
x_i\longrightarrow x_i.
\]
The second branch is not the absence of a rule. Preservation is itself a mathematical requirement. The computation must guarantee that the original value passes into the new state without alteration.
The concrete behavior can be displayed as follows:









Position \(i\)
Original \(x_i\)
Condition \(x_i<20\)
Required updated value \(x_i'\)




\(1\)
\(18\)
true
\(20\)


\(2\)
\(24\)
false
\(24\)


\(3\)
\(16\)
true
\(18\)


\(4\)
\(27\)
false
\(27\)


\(5\)
\(19\)
true
\(21\)



The condition from Chapter 5 can be encoded as the mask component
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i<20].
\]
For the concrete collection,
\[
m_1=1,
\qquad
m_2=0,
\qquad
m_3=1,
\qquad
m_4=0,
\qquad
m_5=1.
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The mask correctly describes where correction is required. It does not yet describe how the corrected state should be constructed.



Chapter 5 used elementwise gating:
\[
y_i=m_ix_i.
\]
If we apply that construction directly to the temperature readings, we obtain
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\odot
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
24\\
16\\
27\\
19
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
18\\
0\\
16\\
0\\
19
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This output identifies the readings requiring correction by preserving them and suppressing the others. It may be useful for some purpose, but it is not the corrected collection. The failure occurs because the gates are controlling the existing values:
\[
m_ix_i.
\]
When \(m_i=0\), the gate produces
\[
0x_i=0.
\]
The update requirement is different. When \(m_i=0\), we need
\[
x_i'=x_i,
\]
not
\[
x_i'=0.
\]
The nonqualifying values must pass unchanged from the original state to the updated state. The selected values also reveal a problem. When \(m_i=1\), the gated expression produces
\[
m_ix_i=x_i.
\]
It preserves the old reading, but the required updated value is
\[
x_i+2.
\]
Thus direct masking fails in both cases:
\[
m_ix_i
=
\begin{cases}
x_i, & m_i=1,\\
0, & m_i=0,
\end{cases}
\]
whereas the update requires
\[
x_i'
=
\begin{cases}
x_i+2, & m_i=1,\\
x_i, & m_i=0.
\end{cases}
\]
The issue is not that the mask is incorrect. The issue is that it has been attached to the wrong mathematical quantity.



Every updated reading contains the original reading as its starting point. For selected positions,
\[
x_i'=x_i+2.
\]
For unselected positions,
\[
x_i'=x_i.
\]
The original value \(x_i\) therefore appears in both cases. It is the persistent part of the state transition. What differs between the two cases is the additional correction:
\[
2
\quad\text{or}\quad
0.
\]
The required correction at each position is
\[
\text{correction at position }i
=
\begin{cases}
2, & m_i=1,\\
0, & m_i=0.
\end{cases}
\]
This reveals a new place for the gate. The condition should not control whether the existing state survives. The existing state must survive in every case. The condition should control whether the proposed change contributes. The update can therefore be decomposed conceptually into two parts:
\[
\boxed{
\text{updated state}
=
\text{original state}
+
\text{conditionally active change}.
}
\]
For the first reading, the original state is \(18\) and the active change is \(2\):
\[
18\longrightarrow18+2=20.
\]
For the second reading, the original state is \(24\) and the inactive change is \(0\):
\[
24\longrightarrow24+0=24.
\]
The value remains unchanged not because the update forgot about it, but because the change applied to it is the additive identity \(0\). This gives zero a different role from the one it played in direct masking. In
\[
m_ix_i,
\]
zero suppresses the existing value. In a selective update, zero should suppress only the change. The original value must remain outside that suppression. The new construction problem is therefore:

How can \(m_i\) produce a change of \(2\) when it equals \(1\) and a change of \(0\) when it equals \(0\), while the original value \(x_i\) remains present in both cases?

Section 6.2 will construct the algebraic relationship that satisfies this requirement.
