title: Chapter 3 — Multiplication as a Gate
section: 3.2 Why Zero Suppresses and One Preserves
text:
3.2 Why Zero Suppresses and One Preserves
In the previous section, we discovered that when \(b_i=1\), the quantity survives. When \(b_i=0\), the quantity disappears from the contribution. If we want to construct such expressions ourselves rather than merely recognize a familiar pattern, we need to understand why the numbers \(0\) and \(1\) have these particular effects under multiplication.
Consider a simpler problem containing no condition at all. Suppose a program has calculated a contribution of \(8\):
contribution = 8
Now suppose we multiply that contribution by different numbers:
print(3 * contribution)
print(2 * contribution)
print(1 * contribution)
print(0 * contribution)
The results are
24
16
8
0
The contribution is the same in every case. What changes is the factor multiplying it:
\[
3(8)=24,\qquad
2(8)=16,\qquad
1(8)=8,\qquad
0(8)=0.
\]
The factor therefore determines what happens to the final quantity. A factor of \(3\), for example, produces three times the quantity. But the final two cases have special importance for conditional computation. Multiplying by \(1\) leaves the quantity exactly as it was, while multiplying by \(0\) removes the contribution completely. These are precisely the two behaviors we need when representing a binary decision.

Mathematical Gates and Mathematical Transformations
Suppose an item has a potential contribution of \(8\), and a condition says that the item should contribute. We need an arithmetic operation that receives \(8\) and returns \(8\). More generally, if the possible contribution is some arbitrary quantity \(x\), we require
\[
\text{result}=x.
\]
If we want to control the quantity through multiplication, we must find a factor \(g\) satisfying
\[
gx=x.
\]
For example, if \(x=8\), we need
\[
g(8)=8.
\]
The factor \(1\) has exactly this behavior because
\[
1(8)=8,
\]
and, in general,
\[
1x=x.
\]
The notable fact here is that multiplication by \(1\) preserves the quantity being controlled. The number \(1\) is called the multiplicative identity. This is exactly what a mathematical gate requires in its open state. If the contribution is supposed to occur, the control mechanism must not accidentally alter its magnitude. If the intended contribution is \(8\), an open gate must produce \(8\), not \(16\), \(4\), or some other value. Therefore a factor such as \(2\) would not merely say “allow this contribution.” It would both allow and modify the contribution.
Now consider the opposite case. The possible contribution is again \(8\), but the condition says that the item must not contribute. What numerical result do we require? Not \(8\), because then the item would still contribute. Not \(-8\), because that would actively subtract something. We require the contribution to become \(0\).
For an arbitrary potential contribution \(x\), we therefore need a factor \(g\) satisfying
\[
gx=0.
\]
The factor \(0\) has exactly this behavior because
\[
0x=0.
\]
This property is sometimes described by saying that zero is an absorbing element for multiplication: once one factor is zero, the entire product becomes zero regardless of the value of the other factor.
The two values
\[
g\in{0,1}
\]
therefore encode exactly the two transformations required by a binary gate:
\[
gx=
\begin{cases}
x, & g=1,\
0, & g=0.
\end{cases}
\]
This gives us a deeper interpretation of the expression introduced in Section 3.1. In
\[
\mathbf{1}[P]x,
\]
the indicator \(\mathbf{1}[P]\) is not merely a numerical label saying whether proposition \(P\) is true or false. Once it participates in multiplication, its value determines which of two transformations is applied to \(x\). The binary value has therefore become operational. It does something to another quantity.


The Same Number Can Have Different Semantic Roles
There is an important distinction here. The symbols \(0\) and \(1\) are ordinary numbers, but their role inside an expression depends on what the expression is trying to accomplish.
Consider
\[
1+1+0+1.
\]
Here the binary values are being added. Their role is contribution to a count. Each \(1\) contributes one unit to the total, while \(0\) contributes nothing.
Now consider
\[
(1)(12)+(1)(7)+(0)(20)+(1)(5).
\]
The same binary values are now being multiplied by quantities. Their role is no longer to supply the magnitude of the contribution. The quantities \(12\), \(7\), \(20\), and \(5\) already supply that information. The binary values determine whether those quantities survive.
This distinction is central to mathematical programming. In conditional counting,
\[
\mathbf{1}[P_i]
\]
is itself the contribution.
In conditional contribution,
\[
\mathbf{1}[P_i]x_i,
\]
the indicator controls another contribution. The same mathematical object can therefore participate in different computational structures depending on the operation surrounding it.


From Binary Gates to More General Multipliers
The special behavior of \(0\) and \(1\) also helps us see what changes when the multiplier is no longer binary. Suppose
\[
gx
\]
uses
\[
g=0.5.
\]
For \(x=8\),
\[
0.5(8)=4.
\]
The quantity has neither been completely preserved nor completely suppressed. It has been scaled. This reveals a larger structure: \(gx\) is fundamentally a multiplication-based transformation of \(x\). The binary gate is the special case in which we restrict
\[
g\in{0,1}.
\]
If we later allow values between \(0\) and \(1\), multiplication can express partial influence rather than an all-or-nothing decision. That idea will eventually appear in weighted combinations, probability, neural networks, attention, and other mathematical systems. For now, however, we should preserve the simpler distinction: a binary gate permits exactly two behaviors—complete suppression or complete preservation.
Section 3.1 showed that multiplication can act as a gate. This section has explained why. The central relationship is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
1x&=x &&\text{preserves the contribution},\\
0x&=0 &&\text{suppresses the contribution}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The deeper idea is that multiplication gives a binary mathematical object the ability to control another numerical quantity. This completes the conceptual purpose of Chapter 3.

title: Chapter 5 — Masks: Turning Many Conditions into One Mathematical Object
text:
Consider five packages whose weights, measured in kilograms, are
weights = [12, 7, 15, 4, 10]
Suppose a package qualifies for a particular transport category when its weight is at least \(10\) kilograms. For one package, the program can evaluate a single comparison:
weight = 12
qualifies = weight >= 10
The comparison produces True because \(12\geq10\). The collection, however, does not contain only one package. The transport requirement must be answered separately for every package:
weights = [12, 7, 15, 4, 10]

for weight in weights:
    if weight >= 10:
        print(1)
    else:
        print(0)
The program produces
1
0
1
0
1
The five outputs are the results of applying the same decision rule to five different objects. The first evaluation asks
\[
12\geq10,
\]
the second asks
\[
7\geq10,
\]
the third asks
\[
15\geq10,
\]
the fourth asks
\[
4\geq10,
\]
and the fifth asks
\[
10\geq10.
\]
These propositions have the respective truth values
\[
\text{True},
\quad
\text{False},
\quad
\text{True},
\quad
\text{False},
\quad
\text{True}.
\]
Their numerical encodings are therefore
\[
1,
\quad
0,
\quad
1,
\quad
0,
\quad
1.
\]
One comparison rule has produced several results because the object to which the rule refers has changed. The expression
\[
x\geq10
\]
does not possess one permanent truth value. Its truth value depends on the value substituted for \(x\). For \(x=12\), the proposition is true; for \(x=7\), it is false. The comparison is therefore better understood as a rule that maps an input value to a truth value:
\[
P(x)=
\begin{cases}
\text{True}, & x\geq10,\\
\text{False}, & x<10.
\end{cases}
\]
A rule of this kind is called a predicate. It is a condition that can be evaluated at different inputs. Each evaluation \(P(x_i)\) produces the answer associated with the particular value \(x_i\). This distinction separates the invariant part of the computation from the varying part. The qualifying rule remains fixed:
\[
x\geq10.
\]
The package value changes:
\[
x_1=12,\quad
x_2=7,\quad
x_3=15,\quad
x_4=4,\quad
x_5=10.
\]
Consequently, the truth value also changes from position to position. The program is repeating one rule, but it is not repeating one result.


To describe this structure mathematically, assign an index to every package weight:
\[
x_1=12,
\qquad
x_2=7,
\qquad
x_3=15,
\qquad
x_4=4,
\qquad
x_5=10.
\]
The purpose of subscript is to identify the position and therefore the particular object about which a decision is being made. The expression \(x_3=15\) means that the third package has weight \(15\) kilograms. The index \(3\) is part of the referential meaning: it connects the quantity to the third package rather than merely presenting an isolated number.
Because there is one condition evaluation for every indexed weight, there must also be one binary decision for every indexed weight. Let \(m_i\) denote the numerical result of asking whether \(x_i\) satisfies the qualifying condition:
\[
m_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & x_i\geq10,\\
0, & x_i<10.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, using indicator notation,
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10].
\]
The index \(i\) acts as a placeholder that allows the same relationship to be instantiated at every position. For the first package,
\[
m_1=\mathbf{1}[x_1\geq10]
=\mathbf{1}[12\geq10]
=1.
\]
For the second package,
\[
m_2=\mathbf{1}[x_2\geq10]
=\mathbf{1}[7\geq10]
=0.
\]
For the third package,
\[
m_3=\mathbf{1}[x_3\geq10]
=\mathbf{1}[15\geq10]
=1.
\]
For the fourth package,
\[
m_4=\mathbf{1}[x_4\geq10]
=\mathbf{1}[4\geq10]
=0.
\]
For the fifth package,
\[
m_5=\mathbf{1}[x_5\geq10]
=\mathbf{1}[10\geq10]
=1.
\]
We have therefore constructed five related binary quantities:
\[
m_1=1,
\qquad
m_2=0,
\qquad
m_3=1,
\qquad
m_4=0,
\qquad
m_5=1.
\]
Notice that every \(m_i\) has two simultaneous dependencies. It depends on the common predicate \(x\geq10\), which determines what qualifying means, and it depends on the corresponding value \(x_i\), which determines whether qualification occurs at position \(i\). Removing either dependency destroys part of the meaning. Without the predicate, a value of \(1\) does not tell us what property is present. Without the index, it does not tell us where that property is present. This is the conceptual step that occurs when a condition is applied to a collection. For a single value, the result is one binary decision:
\[
x\longrightarrow m.
\]
For an indexed collection, the same predicate produces an indexed family of binary decisions:
\[
x_i\longrightarrow m_i
\qquad
\text{for }i=1,2,\ldots,n.
\]
The relationship can be written generally as
\[
\boxed{
m_i=\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)]
\qquad
\text{for }i=1,2,\ldots,n
}
\]
where \(P\) is the shared predicate, \(x_i\) is the value at position \(i\), and \(m_i\) is the binary result associated with that same position.



The index is not merely a device for counting through the values. It preserves correspondence. The decision \(m_1\) belongs to \(x_1\), \(m_2\) belongs to \(x_2\), and in general \(m_i\) belongs to \(x_i\). This relationship is what allows the decisions to control the original values later. Suppose the five numerical decisions were rearranged:
\[
1,\quad1,\quad0,\quad1,\quad0.
\]
They would still contain three ones and two zeroes, just like the original decisions. They would therefore preserve the total number of qualifying packages. Nevertheless, they would no longer describe correctly which packages qualify. A count preserves only how many conditions succeeded:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{5}m_i=3.
\]
Indexed decisions preserve additional information: they record where those successes occurred. This distinction separates aggregation from structure. The sum
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i
\]
compresses many binary decisions into one count. After summation, the positional information has disappeared. The indexed family
\[
m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n
\]
retains that positional information because every decision remains attached to its corresponding index. The program has therefore created something richer than five unrelated Boolean results and more informative than one total count. It has created a decision for every position in the original collection:
\[
\boxed{
x_i
\longleftrightarrow
m_i
}
\]
The double arrow does not claim that \(x_i\) and \(m_i\) are numerically equal. It records their semantic correspondence: \(m_i\) states whether the value at position \(i\) satisfies the predicate. At this stage, the decisions remain written separately as
\[
m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n.
\]
The next mathematical problem is to determine whether these related decisions can be organized into one structured object without losing their positional correspondence. That object will become the mask.

}
\]
The double arrow does not claim that \(x_i\) and \(m_i\) are numerically equal. It records their semantic correspondence: \(m_i\) states whether the value at position \(i\) satisfies the predicate. At this stage, the decisions remain written separately as
\[
m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n.
\]
The next mathematical problem is to determine whether these related decisions can be organized into one structured object without losing their positional correspondence. That object will become the mask.

title: Chapter 5 — Masks: Turning Many Conditions into One Mathematical Object
section: 5.2 When Separate Decisions Become One Object
text:
5.2 When Separate Decisions Become One Object
Section 5.1 produced one binary decision for every package weight:
\[
m_1=1,
\qquad
m_2=0,
\qquad
m_3=1,
\qquad
m_4=0,
\qquad
m_5=1.
\]
These decisions were derived from the indexed weights
\[
x_1=12,
\qquad
x_2=7,
\qquad
x_3=15,
\qquad
x_4=4,
\qquad
x_5=10
\]
through the common relationship
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10].
\]
At this stage, the decisions can be written one after another, but merely writing several numbers beside one another does not explain why they form a single mathematical object. To construct that object, we must identify what the decisions share.
Every \(m_i\) answers the same kind of question:

Does the value at position \(i\) satisfy the qualifying condition?

The predicate is common, the collection is common, and the index system is common. Only the position being examined changes. The decisions are therefore not unrelated binary facts. They are components of one position-dependent relationship.

A Collection Has an Index Structure
The package weights can be organized as the vector
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The bold symbol \(\mathbf{x}\) refers to the complete collection, while \(x_i\) refers to the component at position \(i\). Thus,
\[
x_1=12,
\qquad
x_2=7,
\qquad
\ldots,
\qquad
x_5=10.
\]
A vector is not merely several numbers enclosed by brackets. It is an ordered mathematical object whose components are identified by positions. If the order changes, the vector changes:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix}
\neq
\begin{bmatrix}
7\\
12\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Both vectors contain the same five numerical values, but the values occupy different positions. If the positions refer to five particular packages, rearranging the components changes which weight belongs to which package. The index is therefore part of the object’s meaning, not merely part of its notation.
The binary decisions inherit this same index structure. Because there is one \(m_i\) for every \(x_i\), the decisions can be organized as
\[
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_1\\
m_2\\
m_3\\
m_4\\
m_5
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The bold symbol \(\mathbf{m}\) refers to the complete structured collection of decisions. Each component retains its original correspondence:
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10].
\]
The two vectors can therefore be placed side by side:
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The first component of \(\mathbf{m}\) describes the first component of \(\mathbf{x}\), the second describes the second, and so forth. The relationship is componentwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_1&=\mathbf{1}[x_1\geq10],\\
m_2&=\mathbf{1}[x_2\geq10],\\
m_3&=\mathbf{1}[x_3\geq10],\\
m_4&=\mathbf{1}[x_4\geq10],\\
m_5&=\mathbf{1}[x_5\geq10].
\end{aligned}
\]
The structure of \(\mathbf{m}\) mirrors the structure of \(\mathbf{x}\). There are five data components and five decision components. The position of each decision matches the position of the value about which that decision was made. This organized binary object is called a mask.


Why a Binary Vector Is Not Automatically a Mask
The numerical vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
does not have an intrinsic meaning independent of context. By itself, it is only a vector whose components happen to be zeroes and ones. It becomes a mask over \(\mathbf{x}\) because three relationships have been established. First, every component is produced by a defined predicate:
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10].
\]
The values \(1\) and \(0\) therefore mean “qualifies” and “does not qualify” with respect to a specific condition. Second, every component of \(\mathbf{m}\) corresponds to a component of \(\mathbf{x}\) through the same index:
\[
m_i\longleftrightarrow x_i.
\]
The mask does not merely state that three packages qualify. It states that the packages at positions \(1\), \(3\), and \(5\) qualify. Third, the mask and the data possess compatible structures. In this example, both have five components:
\[
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{5},
\qquad
\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{5}.
\]
The notation \(\mathbb{R}^{5}\) says that \(\mathbf{x}\) has five real-valued components. The notation \(\{0,1\}^{5}\) says that \(\mathbf{m}\) has five components, each selected from the set \(\{0,1\}\). The common exponent \(5\) expresses the structural compatibility that allows each decision to be paired with one data value. A binary collection becomes a mask only relative to the object and predicate it describes:
\[
\boxed{
\text{mask}
=
\text{binary components}
+
\text{predicate meaning}
+
\text{positional correspondence}
}
\]
This is why an arbitrary rearrangement of the mask destroys its meaning even though it preserves the number of zeroes and ones. Consider
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
1\\
0\\
1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Like the original mask, \(\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}\) contains three ones and two zeroes. Nevertheless, its components claim that positions \(1\), \(2\), and \(4\) qualify. Applied to the original package ordering, those claims are false. The count is unchanged, but the correspondence is corrupted. A mask must therefore remain aligned with the collection from which it was constructed.


The Mask Describes a Subset of Positions
There is another way to understand what the mask represents. The package collection has the index set
\[
\mathcal{I}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}.
\]
The symbol \(\mathcal{I}\) represents the available positions rather than the package weights themselves. The condition \(x_i\geq10\) divides these positions into two groups. The qualifying positions are
\[
\mathcal{Q}
=
\{i\in\mathcal{I}:x_i\geq10\}.
\]
For the concrete weights,
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}.
\]
The nonqualifying positions form the complementary subset
\[
\mathcal{I}\setminus\mathcal{Q}=\{2,4\}.
\]
The mask numerically describes membership in \(\mathcal{Q}\):
\[
m_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & i\in\mathcal{Q},\\
0, & i\notin\mathcal{Q}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is the binary representation of the subset \(\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}\) relative to the ordered index set \(\mathcal{I}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\). This representation is sometimes called the indicator vector or characteristic vector of the subset. The terminology emphasizes that the vector records a property of every position:
\[
m_i=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
i\in\mathcal{Q}.
\]
The set notation and the mask notation preserve related but different views of the same structure. The set
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}
\]
lists only the positions that qualify. The mask
\[
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
retains an explicit binary statement for every position, including those that do not qualify. The mask therefore preserves the complete positional frame of the original collection. This is an important philosophical change in representation. The ordinary loop describes a sequence of actions:

inspect the first value, decide; inspect the second value, decide; continue until the collection ends.

The mask describes the completed relationship:

for every position \(i\), \(m_i\) records whether \(x_i\) belongs to the subset defined by the predicate.

The first view emphasizes temporal execution. The second emphasizes a mathematical object whose components simultaneously describe the condition across the collection.


Shape Generalizes Positional Correspondence
For a one-dimensional collection, compatibility can be described through equal length. Both \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{m}\) have five components. In more structured data, length alone is insufficient.
Consider a \(2\times3\) grid of measurements:
\[
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4 & 11 & 7\\
15 & 3 & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Applying the condition \(X_{ij}\geq10\) produces one decision for every row-and-column position:
\[
M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[X_{ij}\geq10].
\]
The resulting mask is
\[
\mathbf{M}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Here, a single index is no longer enough. The component \(M_{ij}\) corresponds to the measurement \(X_{ij}\) at row \(i\) and column \(j\). The mask must preserve both dimensions because both dimensions contribute to the identity of a position.
For example,
\[
M_{1,2}=1
\]
describes
\[
X_{1,2}=11,
\]
whereas
\[
M_{2,1}=1
\]
describes
\[
X_{2,1}=15.
\]
The two mask components have the same numerical value, but they refer to different locations. Their meaning comes from their indices. The data and mask therefore share the same shape:
\[
\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times3},
\qquad
\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{2\times3}.
\]
Shape is the multidimensional generalization of positional correspondence. It states how components are organized and which indices are required to identify them. A mask over an image, matrix, or tensor is meaningful because its index structure corresponds to the index structure of the object it describes.
At this point, the mask has been constructed as a complete mathematical representation of many related decisions:
\[
\boxed{
m_i=\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)]
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_1\\
m_2\\
\vdots\\
m_n
\end{bmatrix}
\in\{0,1\}^{n}.
}
\]
For multidimensional data, the same relationship becomes
\[
\boxed{
M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[P(X_{ij})]
}
\]
with a mask whose shape matches the data. The mask tells us where the predicate holds, but we have not yet used it to transform the corresponding values. The next problem is to connect the binary component \(m_i\) with the numerical component \(x_i\) so that all qualifying values are preserved and all nonqualifying values are suppressed without destroying their positions.

title: Chapter 5 — Masks: Turning Many Conditions into One Mathematical Object
section: 5.3 Applying Many Gates at Once
text:
5.3 Applying Many Gates at Once
The package weights and their mask are
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The mask records where the qualifying condition holds:
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10].
\]
At this point, \(\mathbf{m}\) describes the decisions, but it has not yet acted on the weights. The values \(12\), \(7\), \(15\), \(4\), and \(10\) remain unchanged in \(\mathbf{x}\). We now want to construct a new collection in which qualifying weights retain their values and nonqualifying weights contribute zero. The required output is
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This result must preserve more than the qualifying values. It must preserve their original positions. The value \(12\) must remain at position \(1\), \(15\) at position \(3\), and \(10\) at position \(5\). Positions \(2\) and \(4\) must remain present, but their contributions must become zero. We should not begin by searching for one operation over the complete vectors. First, we must determine what has to happen at one position.

Reconstructing the Scalar Gate at Each Position
At position \(1\), the value is
\[
x_1=12
\]
and the decision is
\[
m_1=1.
\]
Because the package qualifies, the required output is
\[
y_1=12.
\]
Chapter 3 established that multiplication by \(1\) preserves a numerical contribution:
\[
1x=x.
\]
Therefore,
\[
y_1=m_1x_1=1(12)=12.
\]
At position \(2\), the value is
\[
x_2=7
\]
and the decision is
\[
m_2=0.
\]
Because this package does not qualify, the required output is
\[
y_2=0.
\]
Multiplication by zero suppresses a contribution:
\[
0x=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
y_2=m_2x_2=0(7)=0.
\]
The same reasoning applies independently at every remaining position:
\[
y_3=m_3x_3=1(15)=15,
\]
\[
y_4=m_4x_4=0(4)=0,
\]
and
\[
y_5=m_5x_5=1(10)=10.
\]
The complete componentwise construction is
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1&=m_1x_1=1(12)=12,\\
y_2&=m_2x_2=0(7)=0,\\
y_3&=m_3x_3=1(15)=15,\\
y_4&=m_4x_4=0(4)=0,\\
y_5&=m_5x_5=1(10)=10.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every output component is produced by the gate located at the same position:
\[
\boxed{
y_i=m_ix_i.
}
\]
This equation is the scalar gate from Chapter 3 with an index attached to every quantity. Chapter 3 established
\[
y=mx
\]
for one value and one binary gate. Chapter 5 now establishes
\[
y_i=m_ix_i
\qquad
\text{for }i=1,2,\ldots,n.
\]
The additional index does essential work. It states that \(m_i\) controls \(x_i\) and produces \(y_i\). The gate at one position does not control a value at another position:
\[
m_i\longleftrightarrow x_i\longrightarrow y_i.
\]
The relationship is local to each index.


One Rule Generates the Complete Output
For a general predicate \(P\), the mask component is
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)].
\]
Substituting this definition into the output relationship gives
\[
y_i=\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)]x_i.
\]
This equation combines the condition and the possible contribution at each position. If \(P(x_i)\) is true, then
\[
\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)]=1
\]
and therefore
\[
y_i=1x_i=x_i.
\]
If \(P(x_i)\) is false, then
\[
\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)]=0
\]
and therefore
\[
y_i=0x_i=0.
\]
Thus,
\[
y_i=
\begin{cases}
x_i, & P(x_i)\text{ is true},\\
0, & P(x_i)\text{ is false}.
\end{cases}
\]
For the package condition \(P(x_i)\equiv x_i\geq10\), this becomes
\[
y_i=
\begin{cases}
x_i, & x_i\geq10,\\
0, & x_i<10.
\end{cases}
\]
The indexed equation and the piecewise equation express the same transformation:
\[
\boxed{
y_i
=
\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10]x_i
=
\begin{cases}
x_i, & x_i\geq10,\\
0, & x_i<10.
\end{cases}
}
\]
The piecewise form describes the two possible cases explicitly. The indicator form places the condition inside an algebraic expression. Neither changes the meaning of the computation.


Organizing the Componentwise Relationships
The five separately derived equations can be assembled according to their shared index structure:
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1\\
y_2\\
y_3\\
y_4\\
y_5
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_1x_1\\
m_2x_2\\
m_3x_3\\
m_4x_4\\
m_5x_5
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Substituting the concrete values gives
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1(12)\\
0(7)\\
1(15)\\
0(4)\\
1(10)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This is not one gate acting indiscriminately on a collection. It is a structured family of gates:
\[
m_1\text{ controls }x_1,
\quad
m_2\text{ controls }x_2,
\quad
\ldots,
\quad
m_n\text{ controls }x_n.
\]
Because the same local relationship holds at every position, mathematics provides a compact notation for the complete construction:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
}
\]
The symbol \(\odot\) denotes elementwise multiplication, also called the Hadamard product. Its meaning is defined by
\[
(\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x})_i=m_ix_i.
\]
The subscripted definition is more fundamental than the compact notation. It tells us what the operation does at each position. The vector equation is a compression of the indexed family
\[
y_i=m_ix_i
\qquad
\text{for every }i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\odot
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1(12)\\
0(7)\\
1(15)\\
0(4)\\
1(10)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The operation is possible because the two vectors possess corresponding component structures:
\[
\mathbf{m}\in\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Each of the \(n\) mask components is paired with one of the \(n\) data components. The result also has \(n\) components:
\[
\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Thus elementwise masking preserves the dimensional structure:
\[
\{0,1\}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
\longrightarrow
\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
The notation states that the operation accepts a binary vector and a numerical vector of compatible size and produces another numerical vector of that size.


Why This Is Not a Dot Product
The expression
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}
\]
must be distinguished from
\[
\mathbf{m}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}.
\]
The first is an elementwise product. It preserves every position:
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
m_1x_1\\
m_2x_2\\
\vdots\\
m_nx_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Its output is a vector.
The dot product multiplies corresponding components and then adds them:
\[
\mathbf{m}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_ix_i.
\]
Its output is one scalar.
For the package data, elementwise masking produces
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The qualifying values remain identifiable by position. In contrast, the dot product produces
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{m}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}
&=1(12)+0(7)+1(15)+0(4)+1(10)\\
&=12+0+15+0+10\\
&=37.
\end{aligned}
\]
The scalar \(37\) is the total weight of the qualifying packages. It no longer records that the contributing weights came from positions \(1\), \(3\), and \(5\). The two operations therefore answer different computational questions:
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}
\]
asks:

What contribution remains at every original position?

Whereas
\[
\mathbf{m}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_ix_i
\]
asks:

What is the total of all surviving contributions?

The distinction can be expressed as
\[
\boxed{
\text{elementwise gating preserves positions},
\qquad
\text{reduction combines positions}.
}
\]
The dot product contains masking as its first local step, but it continues by summing the masked contributions. Elementwise multiplication stops before that reduction.
An ordinary program could construct the masked values procedurally:
weights = [12, 7, 15, 4, 10]
masked_weights = []

for weight in weights:
    if weight >= 10:
        masked_weights.append(weight)
    else:
        masked_weights.append(0)
This code says what to do in time: inspect a value, test it, append either the value or zero, and repeat.
The indexed equation says what relationship holds at every position:
\[
y_i=\mathbf{1}[x_i\geq10]x_i.
\]
The vector equation organizes all those relationships into one transformation:
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\]
These are not three unrelated solutions. They are three levels of description of the same computation:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{procedural description}
&:\quad
\text{visit each position and branch},\\
\text{indexed description}
&:\quad
y_i=m_ix_i,\\
\text{vector description}
&:\quad
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


Extending the Relationship to a Grid
Section 5.2 introduced the measurement grid
\[
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4 & 11 & 7\\
15 & 3 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and its mask
\[
\mathbf{M}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
where
\[
M_{ij}=\mathbf{1}[X_{ij}\geq10].
\]
The required output at every row-and-column position is
\[
Y_{ij}=M_{ij}X_{ij}.
\]
Evaluating these local gates gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{1,1}&=0(4)=0,\\
Y_{1,2}&=1(11)=11,\\
Y_{1,3}&=0(7)=0,\\
Y_{2,1}&=1(15)=15,\\
Y_{2,2}&=0(3)=0,\\
Y_{2,3}&=1(12)=12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Organizing the results in the same shape produces
\[
\mathbf{Y}
=
\mathbf{M}\odot\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\odot
\begin{bmatrix}
4 & 11 & 7\\
15 & 3 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 11 & 0\\
15 & 0 & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The mask does not flatten the grid or discard its coordinate system. Every output remains associated with its original row and column. The general relationship is
\[
\boxed{
Y_{ij}=M_{ij}X_{ij}.
}
\]
The matrix notation
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{M}\odot\mathbf{X}
}
\]
again compresses the family of componentwise gates without changing their positional meaning.

title: Chapter 5 — Masks: Turning Many Conditions into One Mathematical Object
section: 5.4 Masking and Filtering Are Different Transformations
text:
5.4 Masking and Filtering Are Different Transformations
The package weights and their mask are
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
7\\
15\\
4\\
10
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The qualifying positions are
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}.
\]
Section 5.3 applied the mask through elementwise multiplication:
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\]
This produced
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The values at positions \(2\) and \(4\) have been suppressed, but the positions themselves remain present. The output still has five components:
\[
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{5}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{5}.
\]
Another program might use the same qualifying condition differently:
weights = [12, 7, 15, 4, 10]

qualifying_weights = []

for weight in weights:
    if weight >= 10:
        qualifying_weights.append(weight)
This program produces
[12, 15, 10]
In mathematical notation, the resulting collection can be written as
\[
\mathbf{z}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
15\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The outputs \(\mathbf{y}\) and \(\mathbf{z}\) contain the same qualifying numerical values, but they are not the same mathematical object:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
15\\
0\\
10
\end{bmatrix}
\neq
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
15\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The difference is not merely that one output contains zeroes and the other does not. The two transformations preserve different information.

Masking Preserves the Original Index Domain
The original collection is indexed by
\[
\mathcal{I}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}.
\]
Elementwise masking defines an output for every original index:
\[
y_i=m_ix_i
\qquad
\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{I}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
y_1=12,
\qquad
y_2=0,
\qquad
y_3=15,
\qquad
y_4=0,
\qquad
y_5=10.
\]
The output still answers a question about each of the five original positions. At position \(2\), it says that the contribution has been suppressed. At position \(4\), it says the same. The zeroes are not empty spaces. They are numerical results attached to positions that continue to exist. The transformation can be viewed as a function
\[
T_{\mathbf{m}}:\mathbb{R}^{5}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{5}
\]
defined by
\[
T_{\mathbf{m}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\]
The input and output belong to spaces of the same dimension. More generally,
\[
T_{\mathbf{m}}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Masking changes component values while preserving the surrounding coordinate system:
\[
\boxed{
\text{same positions},
\qquad
\text{same order},
\qquad
\text{same length},
\qquad
\text{different contributions}.
}
\]
This is why masking can be described as a structure-preserving form of suppression. It does not preserve every numerical value, but it preserves the frame in which those values are located.


Filtering Restricts the Index Domain
Filtering performs a different operation. It retains only the values whose indices belong to
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}.
\]
The filtered values are
\[
x_1=12,
\qquad
x_3=15,
\qquad
x_5=10.
\]
They can be written as
\[
\mathbf{x}_{\mathcal{Q}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1\\
x_3\\
x_5
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
15\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The notation \(\mathbf{x}_{\mathcal{Q}}\) means that the collection has been restricted to positions in \(\mathcal{Q}\). It is not the result of multiplying the complete vector by binary gates. It is the result of selecting a subset of its components. The transformation now has the form
\[
F_{\mathcal{Q}}:\mathbb{R}^{5}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3},
\]
because three of the five positions qualify. In general, if
\[
|\mathcal{Q}|=q,
\]
then filtering has the form
\[
F_{\mathcal{Q}}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{q},
\]
where \(q\) depends on how many components satisfy the condition. Filtering therefore changes the dimensional description of the collection:
\[
\boxed{
\text{remove excluded positions},
\qquad
\text{retain qualifying values},
\qquad
\text{produce a possibly shorter object}.
}
\]
The predicate is the same in both transformations. The subset \(\mathcal{Q}\) is the same. What differs is the output requirement. Masking asks:

What should remain at every original position after nonqualifying contributions have been suppressed?

Filtering asks:

Which values should remain after nonqualifying positions have been removed?



Zero Is a Value, Not an Absence of Position
The distinction becomes clearer when the original data already contains zero. Consider
\[
\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
7
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and suppose the mask is
\[
\mathbf{r}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Elementwise masking gives
\[
\mathbf{r}\odot\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1(12)\\
1(0)\\
0(7)
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The two output zeroes have different origins. The zero at position \(2\) is a genuine data value preserved by an open gate:
\[
1(0)=0.
\]
The zero at position \(3\) is produced by suppressing a nonzero value:
\[
0(7)=0.
\]
The masked output alone does not distinguish these histories. Both results are numerically zero. The mask must be retained if the distinction between “originally zero” and “suppressed to zero” matters. This shows why zero should not be interpreted as a missing position. Under masking, zero is a value occupying a position. It may arise from the original data or from a closed gate. In either case, the position remains part of the output. Filtering avoids introducing suppressed zeroes because it removes excluded positions:
\[
\mathbf{a}_{\mathcal{R}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
0
\end{bmatrix},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{R}=\{1,2\}.
\]
The genuine zero remains because its position qualifies. The value \(7\) disappears because its position does not qualify.


Filtering Creates a New Positional System
The filtered vector
\[
\mathbf{z}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
12\\
15\\
10
\end{bmatrix}
\]
has three output positions. If these are labeled consecutively, then
\[
z_1=12,
\qquad
z_2=15,
\qquad
z_3=10.
\]
But the original positions were
\[
x_1=12,
\qquad
x_3=15,
\qquad
x_5=10.
\]
Thus the second component of the filtered vector came from the third component of the original vector. The third filtered component came from the fifth original component. Filtering therefore introduces a mapping between the new index system and the old one. If the ordered qualifying indices are
\[
q_1=1,
\qquad
q_2=3,
\qquad
q_3=5,
\]
then the filtered output satisfies
\[
z_j=x_{q_j}
\qquad
\text{for }j=1,2,3.
\]
More generally, if
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_q\}
\]
with the indices written in their retained order, then
\[
\boxed{
z_j=x_{q_j}
\qquad
\text{for }j=1,2,\ldots,q.
}
\]
This equation exposes a structural fact that ordinary filtering syntax can hide. The output index \(j\) and the original index \(q_j\) are not necessarily the same. Filtering compresses the surviving components into a new collection. If the original locations will be needed later, the values alone are insufficient. The indices must also be retained:
\[
(q_j,z_j).
\]
For the package example, this gives
\[
(1,12),
\qquad
(3,15),
\qquad
(5,10).
\]
Without the original indices, the filtered vector preserves the qualifying values and their relative order, but it does not by itself preserve their absolute positions in the original collection.


The Same Predicate Can Support Different Mathematical Objectives
Both masking and filtering begin with
\[
m_i=\mathbf{1}[P(x_i)].
\]
The mask records where the predicate holds. What happens next depends on what the computation must preserve. If the requirement is

keep the original structure but eliminate nonqualifying contributions,

then the appropriate relationship is
\[
y_i=m_ix_i
\]
or
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\]
If the requirement is

construct a collection containing only qualifying values,

then the appropriate relationship is
\[
z_j=x_{q_j},
\]
where \(q_j\) is the original index of the \(j\)th qualifying value. This distinction can be summarized exactly:



Property
Masking
Filtering




Uses the predicate
Yes
Yes


Uses qualifying positions
Yes
Yes


Preserves original length
Yes
Not necessarily


Preserves every original position
Yes
No


Replaces excluded values by zero
Yes
No


Removes excluded positions
No
Yes


Produces a new index system
No
Usually


Retains original locations without extra information
Yes
No





The Distinction Becomes More Important in Higher Dimensions
Consider the measurement grid
\[
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4 & 11 & 7\\
15 & 3 & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and its mask
\[
\mathbf{M}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Elementwise masking gives
\[
\mathbf{M}\odot\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 11 & 0\\
15 & 0 & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The result remains a \(2\times3\) grid. The values \(11\), \(15\), and \(12\) remain at coordinates \((1,2)\), \((2,1)\), and \((2,3)\). The spatial organization is preserved. Filtering the same grid by the same condition could instead produce the one-dimensional collection
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
11\\
15\\
12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The qualifying values remain, but the \(2\times3\) grid structure has disappeared. From this vector alone, we cannot determine that \(11\) came from coordinate \((1,2)\) or that \(12\) came from coordinate \((2,3)\).
If the coordinates matter, they must be retained separately:
\[
((1,2),11),
\qquad
((2,1),15),
\qquad
((2,3),12).
\]
This is why masking is especially important for images, spatial measurements, matrices, and tensors. A zeroed image region remains located inside the image. A filtered list of pixel values no longer possesses the original image geometry. The mathematical choice therefore depends on what kind of meaning the structure carries. If position represents time, space, identity, or correspondence with another collection, removing positions may destroy information that the computation still needs.


A Mask Is a Description Before It Is an Action
The mask
\[
\mathbf{m}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0\\
1\\
0\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
first describes the subset
\[
\mathcal{Q}=\{1,3,5\}.
\]
That same description can support several later operations. It can suppress excluded contributions:
\[
\mathbf{m}\odot\mathbf{x}.
\]
It can count qualifying positions:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i.
\]
It can total qualifying values:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_ix_i.
\]
It can also determine which positions should be extracted into a filtered collection. The mask and the operation performed with it must therefore be distinguished. The mask answers:

Where does the predicate hold?

The subsequent operation answers:

What should be done with that positional information?

This separation prevents the word mask from being reduced to one library operation. Mathematically, a mask is a structured binary representation of membership across an indexed domain. Multiplication, counting, summation, filtering, and later selective updating are different uses of that representation.
A mask is not merely a row of Boolean values produced by a programming library. It is the characteristic representation of a subset over an indexed domain. Its components preserve the connection between a predicate and the positions where that predicate holds. Once this object has been constructed, the programmer can decide whether the computation should preserve the original structure, reduce contributions, extract a subset, or later modify selected values.

title: Chapter 9 — From Element-by-Element Thinking to Vector Thinking
text:
Consider four positions measured in a local coordinate system:
local_positions = [1, 4, -2, 5]
Suppose the corresponding global coordinate is obtained by scaling each local position by \(2\) and then translating it by \(3\):
global_positions = []

for position in local_positions:
    transformed = 2 * position + 3
    global_positions.append(transformed)
The program produces
[5, 11, -1, 13]
A procedural reading emphasizes the sequence of execution. The program takes the first value, transforms it, appends the result, returns to the beginning of the loop, and repeats the process for the next value. From this viewpoint, the computation appears to be a sequence of four actions:
\[
1\longrightarrow5,
\]
then
\[
4\longrightarrow11,
\]
then
\[
-2\longrightarrow-1,
\]
and finally
\[
5\longrightarrow13.
\]
This description is correct, but it combines two different kinds of information. It describes both the mathematical relationship between an input and its output and the order in which a particular machine happens to construct the outputs. To move toward vector thinking, these ideas must be separated.


The first result is calculated as
\[
2(1)+3=5.
\]
The second is calculated as
\[
2(4)+3=11.
\]
The third is calculated as
\[
2(-2)+3=-1.
\]
The fourth is calculated as
\[
2(5)+3=13.
\]
The computation of \(11\) does not use the previously computed value \(5\). The computation of \(-1\) does not use \(5\) or \(11\). The computation of \(13\) does not depend on any earlier result. Each output requires only one corresponding input and the common transformation rule.
This means that the temporal statement

the computer calculates the first output before the second output

does not imply the mathematical statement

the second output depends on the first output.

These are different relationships. Execution order describes when operations occur. Mathematical dependence describes which quantities are required to determine another quantity. A program may choose a sequential execution order even when no mathematical dependency forces that order. The loop gives the computer an itinerary through the collection:
\[
1\rightarrow2\rightarrow3\rightarrow4.
\]
The transformation rule gives the mathematical dependency at each position:
\[
\text{output at position }i
\longleftarrow
\text{input at position }i.
\]
The itinerary is a property of the procedure. The dependency is a property of the computation being represented.



Let the local positions be denoted by
\[
x_1=1,
\qquad
x_2=4,
\qquad
x_3=-2,
\qquad
x_4=5.
\]
Let the corresponding global positions be
\[
y_1=5,
\qquad
y_2=11,
\qquad
y_3=-1,
\qquad
y_4=13.
\]
The subscript \(i\) identifies a position in the collection. The value \(x_i\) is the input at position \(i\), while \(y_i\) is the output at that same position. The four calculations can now be written as
\[
y_1=2x_1+3,
\]
\[
y_2=2x_2+3,
\]
\[
y_3=2x_3+3,
\]
and
\[
y_4=2x_4+3.
\]
The equations differ only in their subscripts. Their mathematical structure is identical. Instead of writing the relationship four times, we can use an arbitrary index \(i\):
\[
\boxed{
y_i=2x_i+3
\qquad
\text{for }i=1,2,3,4.
}
\]
The index \(i\) does not represent one additional numerical input to the transformation. It identifies which corresponding input-output pair is under consideration. The relationship
\[
y_i=2x_i+3
\]
states that whichever position is chosen, its output is obtained by applying the same rule to its input. This is the first movement from element-by-element thinking toward structural thinking. The loop says:

Repeat this instruction for every element.

The indexed equation says:

This relationship holds at every position.

The two statements describe the same local computations, but they organize the meaning differently.



The transformation applied to one numerical value is
\[
f(x)=2x+3.
\]
Each loop iteration instantiates this same rule at a different input:
\[
y_1=f(x_1),
\]
\[
y_2=f(x_2),
\]
\[
y_3=f(x_3),
\]
\[
y_4=f(x_4).
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
y_i=f(x_i)
\qquad
\text{for every }i.
}
\]
The function \(f\) is invariant across the collection. The values \(x_i\) vary by position. The resulting values \(y_i\) vary because the same function receives different inputs. This distinction identifies two mathematical roles:
\[
f
=
\text{the shared transformation},
\]
whereas
\[
x_i
=
\text{the position-specific input}.
\]
The loop does not create four unrelated transformation rules. It applies one rule four times. The source code makes this visible because the loop body remains unchanged:
transformed = 2 * position + 3
Only the value bound to position changes from one iteration to the next. Mathematically, the unchanged loop body corresponds to the shared function \(f\), while the successive bindings correspond to \(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\).



To understand the structure more precisely, change only the second local position:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
4\\
-2\\
5
\end{bmatrix}
\longrightarrow
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
6\\
-2\\
5
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The transformed second value changes from
\[
2(4)+3=11
\]
to
\[
2(6)+3=15.
\]
The other outputs remain
\[
5,
\qquad
-1,
\qquad
13.
\]
The new output collection is therefore
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
5\\
15\\
-1\\
13
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Changing \(x_2\) changes \(y_2\), but it does not change \(y_1\), \(y_3\), or \(y_4\). This experiment reveals the dependency structure:
\[
x_1\longrightarrow y_1,
\]
\[
x_2\longrightarrow y_2,
\]
\[
x_3\longrightarrow y_3,
\]
\[
x_4\longrightarrow y_4.
\]
There are no cross-position dependencies such as
\[
x_1\longrightarrow y_2
\]
or
\[
x_3\longrightarrow y_4.
\]
For this transformation, each output is local to its corresponding input. This property can be stated generally:
\[
\boxed{
y_i\text{ depends on }x_i
\text{ but not on }x_j\text{ for }j\neq i.
}
\]
A transformation with this property is called elementwise. The term means that the transformation acts on each element according to the same local rule without requiring values from other positions.
The term should not be confused with the order in which a program performs the operations. A program may calculate elementwise outputs sequentially, simultaneously, in parallel groups, or in another order. As long as every \(y_i\) is determined by the corresponding \(x_i\) through the same rule, the mathematical relationship remains elementwise.



Suppose the four outputs were calculated in the order
\[
4,\ 2,\ 1,\ 3.
\]
The calculations would be
\[
y_4=2x_4+3=13,
\]
\[
y_2=2x_2+3=11,
\]
\[
y_1=2x_1+3=5,
\]
and
\[
y_3=2x_3+3=-1.
\]
The execution order has changed, but the correspondence between each \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) has not. Once the results are placed at their associated positions, the output remains
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
5\\
11\\
-1\\
13
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This shows that the transformation does not mathematically require the original left-to-right order. What must be preserved is not the order of calculation but the association
\[
x_i\longleftrightarrow y_i.
\]
The computation can be reorganized because its outputs are independent. However, the collection itself is still ordered. Independence does not mean that positions can be confused. The value calculated from \(x_4\) must still become \(y_4\), even if it is calculated first. This distinction is essential:
\[
\boxed{
\text{the order of execution may change,
but the index correspondence must not.}
}
\]



The loop presents the transformation as a process unfolding through time:
read one value
transform it
store the result
move to the next value
The indexed equation presents the same computation as a completed family of relationships:
\[
y_i=2x_i+3
\qquad
\text{for every }i.
\]
The phrase “for every \(i\)” does not claim that a physical computer evaluates all positions at exactly the same instant. It states that the same mathematical relationship is valid throughout the index domain. This is the sense in which the relationship can be understood simultaneously. All four equations belong to one definition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1&=2x_1+3,\\
y_2&=2x_2+3,\\
y_3&=2x_3+3,\\
y_4&=2x_4+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
The loop is one possible procedure for realizing that definition. It is not the definition itself. For the current computation:
\[
\text{loop}
=
\text{construction procedure},
\]
while
\[
y_i=f(x_i)
=
\text{completed input-output relationship}.
\]



The original program appears to act on four separate numbers. Yet these numbers are not unrelated. They belong to one indexed collection:
\[
x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4.
\]
The outputs likewise belong to one indexed collection:
\[
y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4.
\]
The transformation preserves the correspondence between the two collections:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1&\longrightarrow y_1,\\
x_2&\longrightarrow y_2,\\
x_3&\longrightarrow y_3,\\
x_4&\longrightarrow y_4.
\end{aligned}
\]
This permits a change in the object of thought. Instead of thinking:

I have four numbers, and I must perform an operation four times,

we can begin to think:

I have one structured collection, and one relationship determines its corresponding output collection.

The first viewpoint treats repetition as the primary fact. The second treats common structure as the primary fact.
The movement can be summarized as
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{procedural view}
&:\quad
\text{visit }x_1,\text{ then }x_2,\text{ then }x_3,\text{ then }x_4,\\
\text{indexed view}
&:\quad
y_i=f(x_i)\text{ for every }i.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
We have not yet written the complete input collection or output collection as a single vector transformation. That step requires us to determine how a scalar function \(f\) can be extended, or lifted, from one value to an indexed collection. The important foundation has now been established: the repeated loop body represents one common relationship, and the outputs are linked to their corresponding inputs by index rather than by execution order.

\end{bmatrix}.
\]
This shows that the transformation does not mathematically require the original left-to-right order. What must be preserved is not the order of calculation but the association
\[
x_i\longleftrightarrow y_i.
\]
The computation can be reorganized because its outputs are independent. However, the collection itself is still ordered. Independence does not mean that positions can be confused. The value calculated from \(x_4\) must still become \(y_4\), even if it is calculated first. This distinction is essential:
\[
\boxed{
\text{the order of execution may change,
but the index correspondence must not.}
}
\]



The loop presents the transformation as a process unfolding through time:
read one value
transform it
store the result
move to the next value
The indexed equation presents the same computation as a completed family of relationships:
\[
y_i=2x_i+3
\qquad
\text{for every }i.
\]
The phrase “for every \(i\)” does not claim that a physical computer evaluates all positions at exactly the same instant. It states that the same mathematical relationship is valid throughout the index domain. This is the sense in which the relationship can be understood simultaneously. All four equations belong to one definition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_1&=2x_1+3,\\
y_2&=2x_2+3,\\
y_3&=2x_3+3,\\
y_4&=2x_4+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
The loop is one possible procedure for realizing that definition. It is not the definition itself. For the current computation:
\[
\text{loop}
=
\text{construction procedure},
\]
while
\[
y_i=f(x_i)
=
\text{completed input-output relationship}.
\]



The original program appears to act on four separate numbers. Yet these numbers are not unrelated. They belong to one indexed collection:
\[
x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4.
\]
The outputs likewise belong to one indexed collection:
\[
y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4.
\]
The transformation preserves the correspondence between the two collections:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1&\longrightarrow y_1,\\
x_2&\longrightarrow y_2,\\
x_3&\longrightarrow y_3,\\
x_4&\longrightarrow y_4.
\end{aligned}
\]
This permits a change in the object of thought. Instead of thinking:

I have four numbers, and I must perform an operation four times,

we can begin to think:

I have one structured collection, and one relationship determines its corresponding output collection.

The first viewpoint treats repetition as the primary fact. The second treats common structure as the primary fact.
The movement can be summarized as
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{procedural view}
&:\quad
\text{visit }x_1,\text{ then }x_2,\text{ then }x_3,\text{ then }x_4,\\
\text{indexed view}
&:\quad
y_i=f(x_i)\text{ for every }i.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
We have not yet written the complete input collection or output collection as a single vector transformation. That step requires us to determine how a scalar function \(f\) can be extended, or lifted, from one value to an indexed collection. The important foundation has now been established: the repeated loop body represents one common relationship, and the outputs are linked to their corresponding inputs by index rather than by execution order.

title: Chapter 9 — From Element-by-Element Thinking to Vector Thinking
section: 9.2 Lifting a Scalar Rule to a Collection
text:
9.2 Lifting a Scalar Rule to a Collection
Consider the following scalar function:
\[
f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.
\]
This notation says that \(f\) accepts one real number and produces one real number. For example,
\[
f(4)=11.
\]
The input \(4\) and output \(11\) are scalars. But our input collection has the domain:
\[
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}.
\]
It contains four real components. Therefore the function \(f\) whose declared domain is \(\mathbb{R}\) does not automatically accept an element of \(\mathbb{R}^{4}\). Therefore, writing
\[
f(\mathbf{x})
\]
requires an additional definition. We must specify what it means to apply the scalar rule to a vector. We should start by defining a new transformation \(F\) by
\[
F(\mathbf{x})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
f(x_1)\\
f(x_2)\\
f(x_3)\\
f(x_4)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The transformation \(F\) has the type
\[
F:\mathbb{R}^{4}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{4}.
\]
It accepts a four-component vector and produces a four-component vector. For a general collection of length \(n\), the definition becomes
\[
\boxed{
F(\mathbf{x})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
f(x_1)\\
f(x_2)\\
\vdots\\
f(x_n)
\end{bmatrix}.
}
\]
Its domain and codomain are
\[
F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
The transformation \(F\) is called the coordinatewise lifting or elementwise lifting of \(f\). The word lifting describes the movement from a rule over individual values to a corresponding rule over a structured collection:
\[
\boxed{
f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}.
}
\]
The scalar rule has not been replaced. It has been preserved at every coordinate:
\[
(F(\mathbf{x}))_i=f(x_i).
\]
The notation \((F(\mathbf{x}))_i\) means the \(i\)th component of the output produced by \(F\). This equation is the defining property of the lifted transformation.

Constructing the Compact Vector Expression
Consider the following the scalar rule
\[
f(x)=2x+3,
\]
and the lifted transformation is
\[
F(\mathbf{x})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2x_1+3\\
2x_2+3\\
\vdots\\
2x_n+3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The scaling part can be written as
\[
2\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2x_1\\
2x_2\\
\vdots\\
2x_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
To add \(3\) to every component, introduce the vector of ones
\[
\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
1\\
\vdots\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Then
\[
3\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
3\\
\vdots\\
3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Adding these vectors componentwise gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\mathbf{x}+3\mathbf{1}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
2x_1\\
2x_2\\
\vdots\\
2x_n
\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
3\\
\vdots\\
3
\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
2x_1+3\\
2x_2+3\\
\vdots\\
2x_n+3
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, the lifted transformation can be written compactly as
\[
\boxed{
F(\mathbf{x})=2\mathbf{x}+3\mathbf{1}.
}
\]
Since \(\mathbf{y}=F(\mathbf{x})\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{y}=2\mathbf{x}+3\mathbf{1}.
}
\]
This notation is mathematically explicit. Both terms belong to \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\):
\[
2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},
\]
\[
3\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Programming libraries often permit the shorter expression
y = 2 * x + 3
where the scalar \(3\) is automatically applied to every component. That behavior will later be studied as broadcasting. At the present stage, the vector of ones makes the mathematical operation explicit:
\[
3
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
3\mathbf{1}.
\]
The scalar is converted into a constant vector compatible with the shape of \(\mathbf{x}\).


Shape Preservation Is Part of the Construction
The scalar function maps one value to one value:
\[
f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.
\]
Its elementwise lifting maps \(n\) values to \(n\) values:
\[
F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Thus the transformation preserves the index domain:
\[
\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
\longrightarrow
\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
\]
Every input position has exactly one corresponding output position. No position is removed, no new position is introduced, and no two positions are combined.
This can be expressed as
\[
\boxed{
\text{one input component}
\longrightarrow
\text{one corresponding output component}.
}
\]
For a matrix
\[
\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times c},
\]
an elementwise lifting produces
\[
\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times c}
\]
with
\[
Y_{ij}=f(X_{ij}).
\]
The number of rows and columns is preserved because the transformation acts on values without changing the coordinate system that organizes them.
For example, if
\[
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 4\\
-2 & 5
\end{bmatrix},
\]
then the lifted transformation produces
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(\mathbf{X})
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
f(1) & f(4)\\
f(-2) & f(5)
\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
5 & 11\\
-1 & 13
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The output at row \(i\) and column \(j\) depends on the input at the same row and column:
\[
Y_{ij}=f(X_{ij}).
\]
The lifting preserves structure because it preserves index correspondence.


From Repetition to a Transformation of One Object
The original loop was
global_positions = []

for position in local_positions:
    transformed = 2 * position + 3
    global_positions.append(transformed)
A procedural reading sees repeated execution:
\[
\text{apply }f,
\quad
\text{apply }f,
\quad
\text{apply }f,
\quad
\text{apply }f.
\]
The indexed reading sees one relationship instantiated at every position:
\[
y_i=f(x_i).
\]
The lifted reading sees one transformation between structured objects:
\[
\mathbf{y}=F(\mathbf{x}).
\]
These descriptions can be organized as
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{scalar rule}
&:\quad
y=f(x),\\
\text{indexed family}
&:\quad
y_i=f(x_i),\\
\text{lifted transformation}
&:\quad
\mathbf{y}=F(\mathbf{x}),\\
\text{defining correspondence}
&:\quad
(F(\mathbf{x}))_i=f(x_i).
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The vector transformation does not deny that individual components exist. It incorporates their repeated relationship into the definition of one higher-level object. This is the central movement from element-by-element thinking to vector thinking.

title: Chapter 9 — From Element-by-Element Thinking to Vector Thinking
section: 9.3 Independent and Coupled Transformations
text:
9.3 Independent and Coupled Transformations
The transformations studied so far have had the componentwise form
\[
y_i=f_i(x_i).
\]
Each output component depends on the input at the corresponding position. If \(x_i\) changes while every other input remains fixed, then only \(y_i\) can change. This local dependency makes it possible to understand the complete transformation as a collection of independent scalar relationships.
Not every transformation of a vector has this structure.
A collection may be transformed according to a quantity computed from all of its components. An output at one position may depend on neighboring positions, a shared total, an average, or a weighted combination of the complete input. In such cases, the vector must be treated not merely as a container of separate values but as an interconnected mathematical object.
The central question becomes:

What information from the input is required to determine one output component?

This question reveals whether the transformation is independent or coupled.

A Shared Reference Couples the Outputs
Consider the following requirement:

Express every value relative to the mean of the collection.

For
\[
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
4\\
9
\end{bmatrix},
\]
the mean is
\[
\mu(\mathbf{x})
=
\frac{2+4+9}{3}
=
5.
\]
The centered values are
\[
y_i=x_i-\mu(\mathbf{x}).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2-5\\
4-5\\
9-5
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-3\\
-1\\
4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The subtraction is performed at every position, but the transformation is not independent. To calculate \(y_2\), we need
\[
x_2
\]
and
\[
\mu(\mathbf{x}).
\]
The mean depends on all input components:
\[
\mu(\mathbf{x})
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j.
\]
Thus the component equation is
\[
\boxed{
y_i
=
x_i
-
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j.
}
\]
The index \(i\) identifies the output position. The index \(j\) ranges across the complete input collection. The transformation is therefore coupled. A coupled transformation creates dependencies across positions:
\[
\boxed{
y_i\text{ may depend on }x_j
\text{ even when }j\neq i.
}
\]


Centering as a Vector Transformation
Let
\[
\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
1\\
\vdots\\
1
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
The centered vector can be written as
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{x}
-
\mu(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{1}.
}
\]
The scalar \(\mu(\mathbf{x})\) is converted into a constant vector:
\[
\mu(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu(\mathbf{x})\\
\mu(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\mu(\mathbf{x})
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The subtraction is then componentwise:
\[
y_i=x_i-\mu(\mathbf{x}).
\]
The vector expression contains two structurally different operations:

many input components are combined into one scalar mean;
that scalar is applied across all output positions.

The transformation cannot be described merely as “perform subtraction on every element.” The subtracted quantity is itself a function of the entire vector. This distinction prepares a broader pattern:
\[
\boxed{
\text{reduce the collection}
\rightarrow
\text{use the reduced quantity throughout the collection}.
}
\]
Many normalization, standardization, probability, and machine-learning operations have this form.


Neighboring Dependence Creates Local Coupling
Coupling does not always involve the complete collection. An output may depend on a local neighborhood. Consider a one-dimensional smoothing rule:
\[
y_i
=
\frac{x_{i-1}+x_i+x_{i+1}}{3}.
\]
The output at position \(i\) depends on three input positions:
\[
x_{i-1},
\qquad
x_i,
\qquad
x_{i+1}.
\]
Changing \(x_i\) may affect not only \(y_i\) but also the neighboring outputs
\[
y_{i-1}
\]
and
\[
y_{i+1},
\]
because their neighborhoods also contain \(x_i\). This transformation is not globally coupled in the same way as mean-centering. A distant input may have no effect on \(y_i\). Nevertheless, it is not elementwise because the output requires more than its corresponding input. We can distinguish three dependency patterns:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{elementwise}
&:\quad y_i\text{ depends only on }x_i,\\
\text{locally coupled}
&:\quad y_i\text{ depends on a neighborhood of }i,\\
\text{globally coupled}
&:\quad y_i\text{ may depend on the complete collection}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
These categories describe mathematical dependence, not a particular implementation. A locally coupled transformation may be implemented with loops, convolution operations, matrix multiplication, or specialized hardware. The dependency pattern remains the same.


Matrices Express General Linear Coupling
A broad family of vector transformations can be written as
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x},
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},
\qquad
\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},
\qquad
\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.
\]
To discover the dependency of one output, take the \(i\)th component:
\[
\boxed{
y_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}x_j.
}
\]
The row index \(i\) identifies the output. The column index \(j\) ranges across the inputs that may contribute to that output.
If
\[
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 2 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 2
\end{bmatrix},
\]
then
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}
\]
means
\[
y_1=2x_1,
\]
\[
y_2=2x_2,
\]
and
\[
y_3=2x_3.
\]
The diagonal matrix produces an independent transformation because each row contains only one nonzero coefficient at the corresponding position.
If instead
\[
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
then
\[
y_1=x_1+x_2,
\]
\[
y_2=x_2+x_3,
\]
and
\[
y_3=x_1+x_3.
\]
Each output combines multiple inputs. The transformation is coupled. The vector notation
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}
\]
therefore does not by itself tell us whether the transformation is independent. The structure of \(\mathbf{A}\) determines the dependencies. A diagonal matrix preserves coordinate independence. Off-diagonal nonzero entries create cross-position influence.


Dependency Can Be Represented by Sensitivity
For a differentiable transformation, dependency can also be examined through partial derivatives. If
\[
\mathbf{y}=F(\mathbf{x}),
\]
then
\[
\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}
\]
measures how \(y_i\) responds to a change in \(x_j\). For an elementwise transformation
\[
y_i=f_i(x_i),
\]
we have
\[
\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}=0
\qquad
\text{when }i\neq j.
\]
Changing an input at another position has no local effect on \(y_i\). The matrix of all such sensitivities is the Jacobian:
\[
J_{ij}
=
\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}.
\]
For an elementwise transformation, the Jacobian is diagonal:
\[
\mathbf{J}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1} & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
0 & \frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{\partial y_n}{\partial x_n}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For a coupled transformation, off-diagonal entries may be nonzero:
\[
\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}\neq0
\qquad
\text{for some }i\neq j.
\]
The Jacobian is not required to recognize ordinary vector transformations, but it provides a precise mathematical representation of dependency. Its structure records which inputs can influence which outputs. This idea later becomes important in optimization, automatic differentiation, neural networks, dynamical systems, and sensitivity analysis.


Vectorization Does Not Mean Elementwise Independence
The word vectorized is often used informally to mean that code operates on arrays without an explicit Python loop. This implementation-level meaning must not be confused with mathematical independence.
Both of the following are vector transformations:
\[
\mathbf{y}=2\mathbf{x}+3\mathbf{1}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{x}
-
\mu(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{1}.
\]
The first is elementwise. The second is coupled through the mean. Both may be written compactly in a numerical programming library:
y = 2 * x + 3
and
y = x - x.mean()
The absence of an explicit loop does not imply that every output depends only on its corresponding input. Vectorized notation describes how the computation is expressed or executed at the collection level. Dependency analysis describes the mathematical relationship among components. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\text{vectorized}
\not\Longrightarrow
\text{elementwise independent}.
}
\]
A reduction, matrix multiplication, convolution, normalization, or attention operation may be vectorized while strongly coupling different positions.


A Procedure for Analyzing Dependency
Given a vector expression
\[
\mathbf{y}=F(\mathbf{x}),
\]
the dependency structure can be determined systematically. First, select an arbitrary output component:
\[
y_i=(F(\mathbf{x}))_i.
\]
Second, expand every vector operation and every intermediate quantity until the expression is written in indexed scalar form. Third, inspect which input indices appear. If the final relationship is
\[
y_i=f_i(x_i),
\]
then the transformation is elementwise. If it contains inputs such as
\[
x_{i-1},
\qquad
x_{i+1},
\]
then it is locally coupled. If it contains a sum or function over all inputs,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}g_j(x_j)
\]
or
\[
h(\mathbf{x}),
\]
then it is globally coupled. For example,
\[
\mathbf{y}
=
\frac{\mathbf{x}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j}
\]
has the component form
\[
y_i
=
\frac{x_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j}.
\]
The numerator is local, but the denominator depends on the complete collection. Every normalized output is therefore coupled to every input contributing to the denominator. The visual appearance of componentwise division does not make the complete transformation independent.
Vector thinking therefore means more than replacing a loop with array syntax. It means treating the collection as a mathematical object, defining a transformation over that object, and understanding how the components of the input determine the components of the output. For an independent transformation,
\[
\boxed{
y_i=f_i(x_i).
}
\]
For a coupled transformation,
\[
\boxed{
y_i
=
g_i(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
}
\]
or, more selectively,
\[
\boxed{
y_i
=
g_i\bigl(\{x_j:j\in\mathcal{N}(i)\}\bigr),
}
\]
where \(\mathcal{N}(i)\) denotes the set of input positions relevant to output position \(i\).
The important habit is no longer merely to ask:

Is this code using a loop?

The mathematically useful questions are:

What object is being transformed?


What relationship defines one output component?


Which input components does that output depend on?

Once these questions can be answered, imperative code, indexed equations, vector notation, and numerical-array programs become different representations of the same underlying computational structure.

title: Chapter 11 — From Hard Selection to Soft Selection
text:
Consider a robotic joint that can move between two reference angles. Its initial reference angle is \(20^\circ,\) and its final reference angle is \(80^\circ.\) A binary program could choose one of the two angles:
if move_to_final_position:
    angle = 80
else:
    angle = 20
Let the Boolean condition be represented by the binary indicator \(I\in\{0,1\}.\) The algebraic selector is
\[
I(80)+(1-I)(20).
\]
When \(I=0,\) the result is
\[
0(80)+(1-0)(20)=20.
\]
When \(I=1,\) the result is
\[
1(80)+(1-1)(20)=80.
\]
The robot is commanded either to the initial reference angle or to the final reference angle. There is no third possible output. Now suppose the requirement changes. The joint should move gradually from \(20^\circ\) to \(80^\circ\). A control value should describe how far the movement has progressed. At the beginning of the movement, the progress should be \(0.\) At the end, the progress should be \(1.\) Halfway through the movement, the progress should become \(\frac12.\) A quarter of the way through, the progress should become \(\frac14.\) Therefore, the control value must now represent more than two states:
\[
0,
\quad
\frac14,
\quad
\frac12,
\quad
\frac34,
\quad
1,
\]
as well as every intermediate real value between \(0\) and \(1\). But A binary indicator cannot represent this requirement because its domain contains only \(\{0,1\}.\) Instead, the new control value must belong to the interval \([0,1].\) Let this value be denoted by
\[
w\in[0,1].
\]
The symbol \(w\) is no longer a Boolean indicator. It is a graded quantity. Its numerical value records a degree of progress between two endpoints. The binary set \(\{0,1\}\) contains two isolated values. There is no admissible binary value strictly between them. If \(I\in\{0,1\},\) then the statements \(0<I<1\) and \(I=\frac12\) are impossible. This makes binary indicators suitable for propositions:

the condition is false or true;
the gate is closed or open;
the item is excluded or included;
the first branch or the second branch is selected.

These situations require mutually exclusive states. For the robotic joint, a binary selector can represent:
\[
\text{use the initial reference}
\]
or
\[
\text{use the final reference}.
\]
It cannot represent:
\[
\text{move halfway from the initial reference to the final reference}.
\]
The interval
\[
[0,1]
=
\{w\in\mathbb{R}:0\leq w\leq1\}
\]
however contains infinitely many values. The endpoints retain their familiar meanings:
\[
w=0
\quad\text{represents no progress toward the final state},
\]
and
\[
w=1
\quad\text{represents complete progress toward the final state}.
\]
Intermediate values represent partial progress:
\[
w=\frac14
\quad\text{represents one quarter of the movement},
\]
\[
w=\frac12
\quad\text{represents one half of the movement},
\]
and
\[
w=\frac34
\quad\text{represents three quarters of the movement}.
\]
Unlike a Boolean value, \(w\) does not answer only “which state?” It answers “to what degree?” This produces a conceptual transition:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
I\in\{0,1\}
&:\quad
\text{exclusive state},\\
w\in[0,1]
&:\quad
\text{degree between states}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


The angular distance between the two reference positions is
\[
80-20=60^\circ.
\]
If the joint has completed one quarter of this movement, it has traveled
\[
\frac14(60)=15^\circ
\]
from the starting angle. Its position is therefore
\[
20+15=35^\circ.
\]
At half progress, it has traveled
\[
\frac12(60)=30^\circ,
\]
so its angle is
\[
20+30=50^\circ.
\]
At three-quarter progress, it has traveled
\[
\frac34(60)=45^\circ,
\]
so its angle is
\[
20+45=65^\circ.
\]`
The output set is no longer \(\{20,80\}.\) It is the entire interval \([20,80].\) Every admissible progress value should correspond to an admissible intermediate angle. The input and output structures have both changed:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{hard selection}
&:\quad
\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{20,80\},\\
\text{graded transition}
&:\quad
[0,1]\longrightarrow[20,80].
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The first relationship chooses between two isolated outputs. The second must map a continuous interval of control values into a continuous interval of states. Allowing intermediate states does not mean that any progress value may produce any angle. The ordering must be preserved. If \(w_a<w_b,\) then the angle associated with \(w_a\) should not lie farther toward \(80^\circ\) than the angle associated with \(w_b\).
For example, \(\frac14<\frac12,\) so the quarter-progress angle \(35^\circ\) must occur before the halfway angle \(50^\circ.\) The distance traveled should also correspond proportionally to the progress value. Half progress should apply half of the complete displacement. One-quarter progress should apply one quarter of it. Thus the control value \(w\) has a defined semantic role:
\[
\boxed{

\[

\[
w=\frac14.

w=\frac12,

\[
w=\frac34,

A.

A

\boxed{

=
wA+(1-w)B+c.
