\]
The relative position between the endpoints is preserved under a change of reference. This property also depends on the weights summing to one. It shows that the combination respects translation rather than being anchored artificially to zero.

title: Chapter 11 — From Hard Selection to Soft Selection
text:
Consider a robotic joint that can move between two reference angles. Its initial reference angle is \(20^\circ,\) and its final reference angle is \(80^\circ.\) A binary program could choose one of the two angles:
if move_to_final_position:
    angle = 80
else:
    angle = 20
Let the Boolean condition be represented by the binary indicator \(I\in\{0,1\}.\) The algebraic selector is
\[
I(80)+(1-I)(20).
\]
When \(I=0,\) the result is
\[
0(80)+(1-0)(20)=20.
\]
When \(I=1,\) the result is
\[
1(80)+(1-1)(20)=80.
\]
The robot is commanded either to the initial reference angle or to the final reference angle. There is no third possible output. Now suppose the requirement changes. The joint should move gradually from \(20^\circ\) to \(80^\circ\). A control value should describe how far the movement has progressed. At the beginning of the movement, the progress should be \(0.\) At the end, the progress should be \(1.\) Halfway through the movement, the progress should become \(\frac12.\) A quarter of the way through, the progress should become \(\frac14.\) Therefore, the control value must now represent more than two states:
\[
0,
\quad
\frac14,
\quad
\frac12,
\quad
\frac34,
\quad
1,
\]
as well as every intermediate real value between \(0\) and \(1\). But A binary indicator cannot represent this requirement because its domain contains only \(\{0,1\}.\) Instead, the new control value must belong to the interval \([0,1].\) Let this value be denoted by
\[
w\in[0,1].
\]
The symbol \(w\) is no longer a Boolean indicator. It is a graded quantity. Its numerical value records a degree of progress between two endpoints. The binary set \(\{0,1\}\) contains two isolated values. There is no admissible binary value strictly between them. If \(I\in\{0,1\},\) then the statements \(0<I<1\) and \(I=\frac12\) are impossible. This makes binary indicators suitable for propositions:

the condition is false or true;
the gate is closed or open;
the item is excluded or included;
the first branch or the second branch is selected.

These situations require mutually exclusive states. For the robotic joint, a binary selector can represent:
\[
\text{use the initial reference}
\]
or
\[
\text{use the final reference}.
\]
It cannot represent:
\[
\text{move halfway from the initial reference to the final reference}.
\]
The interval
\[
[0,1]
=
\{w\in\mathbb{R}:0\leq w\leq1\}
\]
however contains infinitely many values. The endpoints retain their familiar meanings:
\[
w=0
\quad\text{represents no progress toward the final state},
\]
and
\[
w=1
\quad\text{represents complete progress toward the final state}.
\]
Intermediate values represent partial progress:
\[
w=\frac14
\quad\text{represents one quarter of the movement},
\]
\[
w=\frac12
\quad\text{represents one half of the movement},
\]
and
\[
w=\frac34
\quad\text{represents three quarters of the movement}.
\]
Unlike a Boolean value, \(w\) does not answer only “which state?” It answers “to what degree?” This produces a conceptual transition:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
I\in\{0,1\}
&:\quad
\text{exclusive state},\\
w\in[0,1]
&:\quad
\text{degree between states}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


The angular distance between the two reference positions is
\[
80-20=60^\circ.
\]
If the joint has completed one quarter of this movement, it has traveled
\[
\frac14(60)=15^\circ
\]
from the starting angle. Its position is therefore
\[
20+15=35^\circ.
\]
At half progress, it has traveled
\[
\frac12(60)=30^\circ,
\]
so its angle is
\[
20+30=50^\circ.
\]
At three-quarter progress, it has traveled
\[
\frac34(60)=45^\circ,
\]
so its angle is
\[
20+45=65^\circ.
\]`
The output set is no longer \(\{20,80\}.\) It is the entire interval \([20,80].\) Every admissible progress value should correspond to an admissible intermediate angle. The input and output structures have both changed:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{hard selection}
&:\quad
\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{20,80\},\\
\text{graded transition}
&:\quad
[0,1]\longrightarrow[20,80].
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The first relationship chooses between two isolated outputs. The second must map a continuous interval of control values into a continuous interval of states. Allowing intermediate states does not mean that any progress value may produce any angle. The ordering must be preserved. If \(w_a<w_b,\) then the angle associated with \(w_a\) should not lie farther toward \(80^\circ\) than the angle associated with \(w_b\).
For example, \(\frac14<\frac12,\) so the quarter-progress angle \(35^\circ\) must occur before the halfway angle \(50^\circ.\) The distance traveled should also correspond proportionally to the progress value. Half progress should apply half of the complete displacement. One-quarter progress should apply one quarter of it. Thus the control value \(w\) has a defined semantic role:
\[
\boxed{
w
=
\text{fraction of the complete transition that has been applied}.
}
\]
The problem is not merely to generate numbers between \(20\) and \(80\). It is to preserve a proportional relationship between progress and displacement.

\]
of a complete allocation. The result is scaled toward zero rather than representing a balanced location between the endpoints. Requiring \(u+v=1\) removes this extra scaling. Once \(u=w,\) the requirement forces \(v=1-w.\) The sum-to-one condition ensures that the output is formed from exactly one complete unit of combined influence.
Suppose the two endpoints are equal as \(A=B=K.\) A sensible combination should return the same value \(K\) regardless of \(w\). Substituting gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
wK+(1-w)K
&=\bigl(w+1-w\bigr)K\\
&=1K\\
&=K.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
A=B=K
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
wA+(1-w)B=K.
}
\]
This property depends on the weights summing to one. With arbitrary weights \(u\) and \(v\),
\[
uK+vK=(u+v)K.
\]
The common value is preserved only if \(u+v=1.\) This is one reason normalized weights are mathematically important: they preserve constant inputs.



Assume
\[
A\geq B
\]
and
\[
0\leq w\leq1.
\]
We want to show that
\[
B\leq wA+(1-w)B\leq A.
\]
Begin with the lower bound. Since
\[
A\geq B,
\]
multiplying by the nonnegative weight \(w\) preserves the inequality:
\[
wA\geq wB.
\]
Adding \((1-w)B\) to both sides gives
\[
wA+(1-w)B
\geq
wB+(1-w)B.
\]
The right side simplifies to
\[
wB+(1-w)B=B.
\]
Therefore,
\[
wA+(1-w)B\geq B.
\]
For the upper bound, since
\[
B\leq A
\]
and
\[
1-w\geq0,
\]
we have
\[
(1-w)B\leq(1-w)A.
\]
Adding \(wA\) gives
\[
wA+(1-w)B
\leq
wA+(1-w)A.
\]
The right side simplifies to
\[
A.
\]
Therefore,
\[
wA+(1-w)B\leq A.
\]
Combining the inequalities gives
\[
\boxed{
B
\leq
wA+(1-w)B
\leq
A.
}
\]
If \(B\geq A\), the same reasoning gives
\[
A
\leq
wA+(1-w)B
\leq
B.
\]
Thus, for weights in \([0,1]\), the combined value remains inside the interval determined by the endpoints.
This boundedness is not an accidental numerical pattern. It follows from two requirements:
\[
w\geq0,
\]
\[
1-w\geq0,
\]
and
\[
w+(1-w)=1.
\]
A combination with nonnegative weights summing to one is called a convex combination.
For two scalar endpoints, a convex combination lies between them.



Suppose both endpoints are shifted by the same amount \(c\):
\[
A'=A+c,
\]
\[
B'=B+c.
\]
Their combination is
\[
\begin{aligned}
wA'+(1-w)B'
&=w(A+c)+(1-w)(B+c)\\
&=wA+wc+(1-w)B+(1-w)c\\
&=wA+(1-w)B+\bigl(w+1-w\bigr)c\\
&=wA+(1-w)B+c.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus shifting both endpoints by \(c\) shifts the combined value by exactly \(c\):
\[
\boxed{
w(A+c)+(1-w)(B+c)
=
wA+(1-w)B+c.
}
\]
The relative position between the endpoints is preserved under a change of reference. This property also depends on the weights summing to one. It shows that the combination respects translation rather than being anchored artificially to zero.

title: Chapter 11 — From Hard Selection to Soft Selection
section: 11.3 Moving Along the Difference Between Two Values
text:
11.3 Moving Along the Difference Between Two Values
Section 11.2 constructed the convex combination
\[
C(w)=wA+(1-w)B.
\]
This form describes the result through two complementary contributions:
\[
wA
\]
and
\[
(1-w)B.
\]
The same expression can be reorganized to reveal a different mathematical structure. Distribute \(B\) across the second term:
\[
wA+(1-w)B
=
wA+B-wB.
\]
Group the terms containing \(w\):
\[
wA+B-wB
=
B+wA-wB.
\]
Factor out \(w\):
\[
B+wA-wB
=
B+w(A-B).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
wA+(1-w)B
=
B+w(A-B).
}
\]
The two forms are algebraically equivalent, but they organize the meaning differently.
The expression
\[
wA+(1-w)B
\]
describes complementary shares of two endpoints.
The expression
\[
B+w(A-B)
\]
describes movement from a starting point.

The Difference Is a Directed Displacement
The quantity
\[
A-B
\]
answers:

What must be added to \(B\) to reach \(A\)?

Its defining relationship is
\[
B+(A-B)=A.
\]
Thus \(A-B\) is the complete displacement from \(B\) to \(A\).
For the robotic joint,
\[
B=20,
\]
\[
A=80.
\]
The displacement is
\[
A-B=80-20=60.
\]
Beginning at \(20\) and applying the complete displacement gives
\[
20+60=80.
\]
The order of subtraction matters. The displacement from \(20\) to \(80\) is
\[
80-20=60.
\]
The displacement from \(80\) to \(20\) is
\[
20-80=-60.
\]
These quantities have equal magnitude but opposite direction.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
A-B
=
\text{directed displacement from }B\text{ to }A.
}
\]
The term directed means that the sign records orientation. A positive displacement moves in the increasing numerical direction; a negative displacement moves in the decreasing direction.


The Weight Scales the Displacement
The expression
\[
w(A-B)
\]
does not represent a share of an endpoint. In the displacement form, it represents a share of the complete movement.
For the joint,
\[
A-B=60.
\]
At
\[
w=\frac14,
\]
the applied displacement is
\[
\frac14(60)=15.
\]
Beginning at \(B=20\) gives
\[
20+15=35.
\]
At
\[
w=\frac12,
\]
the applied displacement is
\[
\frac12(60)=30,
\]
so
\[
20+30=50.
\]
At
\[
w=\frac34,
\]
the applied displacement is
\[
\frac34(60)=45,
\]
so
\[
20+45=65.
\]
At
\[
w=1,
\]
the complete displacement is applied:
\[
20+1(60)=80.
\]
The formula is therefore
\[
\boxed{
C(w)
=
\underbrace{B}_{\text{starting point}}
+
\underbrace{w}_{\text{fraction applied}}
\underbrace{(A-B)}_{\text{complete displacement}}.
}
\]
Each factor has a distinct semantic role.


Endpoint Behavior in the Displacement Form
At
\[
w=0,
\]
no displacement is applied:
\[
C(0)=B+0(A-B)=B.
\]
At
\[
w=1,
\]
the complete displacement is applied:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(1)
&=B+1(A-B)\\
&=B+A-B\\
&=A.
\end{aligned}
\]
For
\[
0<w<1,
\]
only a fraction of the displacement is applied.
The selector \(w\) therefore describes progress along the route from \(B\) to \(A\):
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
w=0
&:\quad
\text{at }B,\\
0<w<1
&:\quad
\text{between }B\text{ and }A,\\
w=1
&:\quad
\text{at }A.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


Interpolation
The process of constructing intermediate values between known endpoints is called interpolation.
For scalar endpoints \(A\) and \(B\), linear interpolation is
\[
\boxed{
C(w)=B+w(A-B),
\qquad
0\leq w\leq1.
}
\]
It is called linear interpolation because equal changes in \(w\) produce equal fractions of the complete displacement.
Suppose \(w\) increases by an amount \(\delta\):
\[
w\longrightarrow w+\delta.
\]
The change in the interpolated value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(w+\delta)-C(w)
&=
\left[B+(w+\delta)(A-B)\right]
-
\left[B+w(A-B)\right]\\
&=
\delta(A-B).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
C(w+\delta)-C(w)
=
\delta(A-B).
}
\]
A fixed increase in \(w\) always produces the same fraction of the endpoint displacement. The relationship has a constant rate of change with respect to \(w\):
\[
\frac{dC}{dw}=A-B.
\]
For the joint,
\[
\frac{dC}{dw}=60.
\]
An increase of
\[
0.1
\]
in progress produces an angular change of
\[
0.1(60)=6^\circ.
\]
The linearity lies in the relationship between progress and displacement.


Relative Position Is Preserved
Consider two progress values
\[
w_1
\]
and
\[
w_2.
\]
Their corresponding states are
\[
C(w_1)=B+w_1(A-B)
\]
and
\[
C(w_2)=B+w_2(A-B).
\]
Subtracting gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(w_2)-C(w_1)
&=
\left[B+w_2(A-B)\right]
-
\left[B+w_1(A-B)\right]\\
&=
(w_2-w_1)(A-B).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
C(w_2)-C(w_1)
=
(w_2-w_1)(A-B).
}
\]
The separation between two interpolated states is proportional to the separation between their weights.
If
\[
w_2-w_1=\frac14,
\]
then the states differ by one quarter of the complete displacement:
\[
C(w_2)-C(w_1)
=
\frac14(A-B).
\]
This property explains why the values
\[
0,\quad\frac14,\quad\frac12,\quad\frac34,\quad1
\]
produce equally spaced positions along the interval from \(B\) to \(A\).


Recovering the Progress from an Intermediate Value
For scalar endpoints with
\[
A\neq B,
\]
the interpolation equation can be solved for \(w\).
Begin with
\[
C=B+w(A-B).
\]
Subtract \(B\):
\[
C-B=w(A-B).
\]
Divide by \(A-B\):
\[
\boxed{
w=\frac{C-B}{A-B}.
}
\]
The numerator
\[
C-B
\]
is the displacement from the starting point to the current state.
The denominator
\[
A-B
\]
is the complete displacement from the starting point to the endpoint.
Their ratio is therefore
\[
\boxed{
w
=
\frac{\text{displacement already traveled}}
{\text{complete displacement}}.
}
\]
For the joint angle
\[
C=50,
\]
we obtain
\[
w
=
\frac{50-20}{80-20}
=
\frac{30}{60}
=
\frac12.
\]
The inverse relationship confirms that \(w\) measures relative position between the endpoints.


Reversing the Endpoints Reverses the Parameter
Suppose the same interval is described from \(A\) toward \(B\) rather than from \(B\) toward \(A\).
The original interpolation is
\[
C(w)=wA+(1-w)B.
\]
If the endpoint labels are reversed, the expression becomes
\[
\widetilde{C}(u)=uB+(1-u)A.
\]
The same physical position is obtained when
\[
u=1-w.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde{C}(1-w)
&=(1-w)B+\bigl(1-(1-w)\bigr)A\\
&=(1-w)B+wA\\
&=C(w).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{reversing the endpoints replaces }w\text{ by }1-w.
}
\]
A position one quarter of the way from \(B\) to \(A\) is three quarters of the way from \(A\) to \(B\).
This shows that \(w\) is not an absolute property of the intermediate value. It is relative to an ordered pair of endpoints.


Vector Endpoints
The endpoints need not be scalars. Let
\[
\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
\]
Their displacement is
\[
\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}.
\]
The interpolated point is
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{C}(w)
=
\mathbf{B}
+
w(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}).
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{C}(w)
=
w\mathbf{A}
+
(1-w)\mathbf{B}.
}
\]
For example, let
\[
\mathbf{B}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
2
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
7\\
6
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The complete displacement is
\[
\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
6\\
4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
At
\[
w=\frac12,
\]
the applied displacement is
\[
\frac12
\begin{bmatrix}
6\\
4
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Adding it to \(\mathbf{B}\) gives
\[
\mathbf{C}\left(\frac12\right)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
2
\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4\\
4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The midpoint is therefore
\[
\frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}}{2}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
4\\
4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
As \(w\) varies from \(0\) to \(1\), \(\mathbf{C}(w)\) traces the straight line segment from \(\mathbf{B}\) to \(\mathbf{A}\).
For scalar endpoints, this segment is an interval. For vector endpoints, it is a geometric line segment in \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\).


Interpolation Remains Inside the Segment
When
\[
0\leq w\leq1,
\]
the applied displacement
\[
w(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})
\]
ranges from zero displacement to the complete displacement.
Therefore,
\[
\mathbf{C}(w)
\]
remains on the segment connecting \(\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\).
This is the geometric meaning of a convex combination of two points:
\[
\boxed{
\left\{
w\mathbf{A}+(1-w)\mathbf{B}
:
0\leq w\leq1
\right\}
=
\text{line segment from }\mathbf{B}\text{ to }\mathbf{A}.
}
\]
The nonnegative complementary weights ensure that the point remains between the endpoints.


Weights Outside the Interval
The algebraic expression
\[
C(w)=B+w(A-B)
\]
is defined for values of \(w\) outside \([0,1]\). However, the geometric meaning changes.
Suppose
\[
w>1.
\]
Then more than the complete displacement is applied. For the joint,
\[
w=1.25
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(1.25)
&=20+1.25(60)\\
&=20+75\\
&=95.
\end{aligned}
\]
The result lies beyond the final endpoint \(80\).
Suppose
\[
w<0.
\]
Then the displacement is applied in the opposite direction. For
\[
w=-0.25,
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(-0.25)
&=20-0.25(60)\\
&=20-15\\
&=5.
\end{aligned}
\]
The result lies beyond the starting endpoint \(20\) in the direction away from \(80\).
This behavior is called extrapolation.
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
0\leq w\leq1
&:\quad
\text{interpolation between the endpoints},\\
w<0
&:\quad
\text{extrapolation beyond }B,\\
w>1
&:\quad
\text{extrapolation beyond }A.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The formula has not changed. The domain assigned to \(w\) determines whether the result is interpreted as interpolation or extrapolation.


Complementary Weights During Extrapolation
When
\[
w>1,
\]
the complementary coefficient
\[
1-w
\]
is negative.
For example, if
\[
w=1.25,
\]
then
\[
1-w=-0.25.
\]
The expression becomes
\[
1.25A-0.25B.
\]
The coefficients still sum to one:
\[
1.25+(-0.25)=1,
\]
so the transformation remains translation-consistent. However, the coefficients are no longer both nonnegative.
This distinguishes an affine combination from a convex combination.
An affine combination requires weights summing to one:
\[
u+v=1.
\]
A convex combination additionally requires nonnegative weights:
\[
u\geq0,
\qquad
v\geq0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{convex combination}
=
\text{affine combination with nonnegative weights}.
}
\]
Interpolation uses a convex combination. Extrapolation uses an affine combination whose weights may include a negative value.


A Geometric Interpretation of the Weight
The weight \(w\) can now be understood in three equivalent ways.
In the complementary-share form,
\[
wA+(1-w)B,
\]
it is the share assigned to endpoint \(A\).
In the displacement form,
\[
B+w(A-B),
\]
it is the fraction of the displacement from \(B\) to \(A\).
In the geometric form, it is the coordinate locating a point along the directed line through \(B\) and \(A\).
These interpretations agree because the expressions are algebraically equivalent:
\[
\boxed{
wA+(1-w)B
=
B+w(A-B).
}
\]
The first form emphasizes combination. The second emphasizes movement. The mathematical structure is the same.


The Completed Construction
The section began with two endpoint contributions:
\[
wA+(1-w)B.
\]
Algebraic rearrangement revealed
\[
B+w(A-B).
\]
The difference
\[
A-B
\]
is the complete directed displacement from \(B\) to \(A\). The weight \(w\) scales that displacement.
For
\[
0\leq w\leq1,
\]
the result lies between the endpoints and performs interpolation.
For
\[
w<0
\]
or
\[
w>1,
\]
the result lies outside the endpoint segment and performs extrapolation.
The conceptual relationship is
\[
\boxed{
\text{new state}
=
\text{starting state}
+
\text{scaled displacement}.
}
\]
The equation determines how the endpoints and weight combine. It does not by itself determine what \(w\) means in a particular application. A weight may represent physical proportion, progress through time, uncertainty, responsibility, confidence, or another quantity. The next section will distinguish these interpretations and show why identical algebra does not imply identical semantics.

title: Chapter 11 — From Hard Selection to Soft Selection
section: 11.4 The Same Formula Can Carry Different Meanings
text:
11.4 The Same Formula Can Carry Different Meanings
The previous sections constructed \(C=wA+(1-w)B\) and its equivalent displacement form \(C=B+w(A-B).\) For \(A=80,\) \(B=20,\) \(w=\frac14,\) the result is
\[
\begin{aligned}
C
&=\frac14(80)+\frac34(20)\\
&=20+15\\
&=35.
\end{aligned}
\]
The calculation is unambiguous. The number \(35\) follows from the given endpoints and weights. What does \(35\) represent?
The equation alone cannot answer. The same numerical relationship can arise from several different models of the world. In one model, \(35\) is an actual intermediate state. In another, it is an average of states that occurred at different times. In another, it is an expected value of mutually exclusive outcomes, even though the system never produces \(35\) as an actual outcome. This leads to a fundamental distinction:
\[
\boxed{
\text{algebraic form}
\neq
\text{semantic interpretation}.
}
\]
The algebra states how quantities are combined. The surrounding problem states what those quantities and weights mean.

Interpretation 1: An Actual Intermediate State
For the robotic joint, let \(B=20^\circ\) be the starting angle and \(A=80^\circ\) be the final angle. If \(w=\frac14\) represents one-quarter progress from \(B\) to \(A\), then \(C=35^\circ\) is the joint’s actual commanded position. The joint is not at \(20^\circ\) for part of the calculation and \(80^\circ\) for another part. It is commanded to one intermediate physical state \(35^\circ.\)
The displacement interpretation is \(C=B+w(A-B).\) Here, \(A-B=60^\circ\) is the complete angular displacement and \(w(A-B)=15^\circ\) is the portion already applied. The output \(35^\circ\) belongs to the same state space as the endpoints. It is a genuine point between them. This interpretation is appropriate when intermediate states are physically and conceptually meaningful.


Interpretation 2: A Physical Mixture
Suppose \(A\) and \(B\) represent concentrations of the same substance in two solutions \(A=80\%,\) \(B=20\%.\) Suppose one-quarter of the final mixture comes from solution \(A\) and three-quarters comes from solution \(B:w=\frac14,\) \(1-w=\frac34.\) Under a linear mixture model, the resulting concentration is
\[
\begin{aligned}
C
&=\frac14(80\%)+\frac34(20\%)\\
&=20\%+15\%\\
&=35\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, the weights represent physical shares of the final mixture. The output \(35\%\) is an actual property of the combined material. The equation is valid because the property being modeled is assumed to combine linearly with the mixture proportions. This assumption should not be treated as automatic. Some physical properties do not mix linearly. Temperature, volume, chemical activity, color perception, and other quantities may require additional physical laws or nonlinear models. The formula \(wA+(1-w)B\) describes a physical mixture only when the modeled quantity obeys the required linear relationship. Thus the semantics include an assumption:
\[
\boxed{
\text{mixture shares combine the chosen property linearly}.
}
\]


Interpretation 3: Time Sharing
Suppose a machine operates at power level
\[
A=80\text{ watts}
\]
for one-quarter of a time interval and at
\[
B=20\text{ watts}
\]
for the remaining three-quarters. Its average power over the interval is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar{P}
&=\frac14(80)+\frac34(20)\\
&=35\text{ watts}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The same weighted expression appears: \(\bar{P}=wA+(1-w)B.\) But the machine may never operate at \(35\) watts. Its actual instantaneous states are only
\[
80\text{ watts}
\]
and
\[
20\text{ watts}.
\]
The number \(35\) describes an average across time, not an intermediate instantaneous state. This differs fundamentally from the robotic-joint interpretation:

the joint may actually occupy the intermediate angle \(35^\circ\);
the time-sharing machine may alternate between \(80\) and \(20\) watts without ever occupying \(35\) watts.

The same number can therefore represent either a state or a summary of several states.
The weight now means
\[
w
=
\text{fraction of time spent in state }A.
\]
The complementary weight means
\[
1-w
=
\text{fraction of time spent in state }B.
\]
Their sum is one because the two modes partition the complete time interval.


Interpretation 4: Uncertainty and Expected Value
Suppose a future quantity \(X\) can take one of two mutually exclusive values:
\[
X=
\begin{cases}
80, & \text{with probability }\frac14,\\
20, & \text{with probability }\frac34.
\end{cases}
\]
The expected value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=\frac14(80)+\frac34(20)\\
&=35.
\end{aligned}
\]
Again, the formula is
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=wA+(1-w)B.
\]
Here, \(w\) is neither geometric progress nor physical mixture proportion nor time fraction. It is a probability:
\[
w=P(X=A).
\]
Its complement is
\[
1-w=P(X=B).
\]
The expected value \(35\) is a probability-weighted average over possible outcomes. The actual outcome is still either
\[
80
\]
or
\[
20.
\]
If the experiment is performed once, the result is not necessarily \(35\). Indeed, \(35\) may not be a possible outcome at all. This distinction is essential:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb{E}[X]=35
\quad\not\Longrightarrow\quad
X=35.
}
\]
The expected value is a summary of the probability distribution, not a prediction that the variable must equal its expectation on a particular trial. The uncertainty interpretation therefore differs from interpolation:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{interpolation}
&:\quad
35\text{ is an admissible intermediate state},\\
\text{expectation}
&:\quad
35\text{ summarizes uncertainty over }20\text{ and }80.
\end{aligned}
}
\]


Interpretation 5: Combining Predictions
Suppose two models produce predictions
\[
A=80
\]
and
\[
B=20.
\]
A combined predictor may use
\[
w=\frac14
\]
for the first model and
\[
1-w=\frac34
\]
for the second:
\[
\hat{y}
=
wA+(1-w)B
=
35.
\]
The output \(35\) is a new prediction formed from the two model outputs.
The weight might represent:

a fixed design choice;
validation performance;
estimated reliability;
an input-dependent learned value;
the output of another model.

The weighted prediction has the same algebraic form as interpolation and expectation. Its semantics depend on how the models and weights were constructed. If \(A\) and \(B\) are predicted numerical values, then \(35\) may be an admissible prediction even if neither model produced it individually. If \(A\) and \(B\) are class labels encoded as numbers, directly averaging them may be meaningless. For example, averaging class identifier 1 and class identifier 3 to obtain 2 does not imply that class 2 is a meaningful compromise between the other classes. The values must belong to a space in which the weighted combination has a defined interpretation.


Interpretation 6: A Continuously Controlled Gate
Suppose \(A\) and \(B\) are two candidate computational pathways. A controller produces \(w\in[0,1].\) The output is \(C=wA+(1-w)B.\) When \(w\approx1,\) pathway \(A\) dominates. When \(w\approx0,\) pathway \(B\) dominates. When \(w\approx\frac12,\) both pathways contribute substantially. This structure is often called a soft gate. Unlike a binary gate, it does not necessarily suppress one pathway completely. The two contributions are \(wA\) and \((1-w)B.\) Both may be nonzero when \(0<w<1.\) The word gate emphasizes control over contribution. The word soft indicates that control is graded rather than binary. This structure appears in mixture models, learned routing, neural gates, recurrent networks, attention-like mechanisms, and ensemble systems. The detailed meanings differ across those applications, but the common algebraic skeleton is complementary weighted contribution.


One Number Can Describe Different Ontologies
For the same values
\[
A=80,
\qquad
B=20,
\qquad
w=\frac14,
\]
the result is always
\[
35.
\]
But the object represented by \(35\) changes:









Interpretation
Meaning of \(w\)
Meaning of \(35\)
Must the system actually occupy \(35\)?




Interpolation
fraction of displacement
intermediate state
Yes


Physical mixture
material share
property of mixture
Usually, under the model


Time sharing
fraction of time
temporal average
No


Uncertainty
probability of outcome \(A\)
expected value
No


Model combination
influence assigned to model \(A\)
combined prediction
Depends on output space


Soft gate
activation of pathway \(A\)
blended pathway output
Usually as computed output



These interpretations share the equation
\[
wA+(1-w)B.
\]
They do not share the same ontology—the same account of what kinds of things the quantities represent.
An equation can preserve numerical structure while the meaning of its symbols changes from one application to another.


A Weight Does Not Explain Itself
Seeing
\[
w=0.8
\]
does not tell us whether \(w\) is:

an \(80\%\) mixture proportion;
an \(80\%\) probability;
an \(80\%\) progress value;
an \(80\%\) time allocation;
a learned gate activation;
a manually chosen model weight.

The interval constraint
\[
0\leq w\leq1
\]
is shared by all these interpretations. It does not identify which interpretation applies.
Even the condition
\[
w+(1-w)=1
\]
only states complementarity. It does not state what is being divided into complementary shares.
The semantics must come from the problem definition:
\[
\boxed{
\text{weight value}
+
\text{constraint}
\not\Longrightarrow
\text{weight meaning}.
}
\]
The reader must ask:

What complete quantity is being divided?


What does each share measure?


Why must the shares sum to one?


What does the weighted output represent?



Confidence Is Not Automatically Probability
In machine-learning discussions, a number in \([0,1]\) is often casually called confidence. This word can hide several different mathematical objects.
A gate value
\[
w=0.8
\]
may mean that pathway \(A\) receives \(80\%\) of the combined influence. It does not automatically mean:
\[
P(A\text{ is correct})=0.8.
\]
For the weight to be interpreted as a probability, it must belong to a probability model with defined events and appropriate normalization.
Likewise, a model score may lie between \(0\) and \(1\) without being statistically calibrated. Numerical range alone does not establish probabilistic meaning.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
w\in[0,1]
\quad\not\Longrightarrow\quad
w\text{ is a probability}.
}
\]
Probability is a semantic and mathematical role, not merely a numerical interval.


Soft Selection Does Not Always Approximate Hard Selection
A soft gate is sometimes used as a smooth approximation to a hard decision. As the weight approaches an endpoint,
\[
w\rightarrow1,
\]
the output approaches \(A\):
\[
wA+(1-w)B\rightarrow A.
\]
As
\[
w\rightarrow0,
\]
the output approaches \(B\).
In such a model, soft selection may be a temporary or differentiable substitute for hard selection.
In other applications, the mixture is the intended final behavior. An ensemble may deliberately combine models. A physical mixture may genuinely contain both components. An expected value is not an approximation to one outcome; it is a summary of a distribution.
Thus the phrase soft selection covers at least two purposes:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{soft as approximation}
&:\quad
\text{eventually imitate a hard choice},\\
\text{soft as model}
&:\quad
\text{represent genuine simultaneous influence}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
The purpose must be determined from context.


Why Continuous Weights Matter for Learning
The output
\[
C(w)=wA+(1-w)B
\]
changes continuously with \(w\). Its derivative is
\[
\frac{dC}{dw}=A-B.
\]
A small change \(\delta\) in the weight produces
\[
C(w+\delta)-C(w)=\delta(A-B).
\]
This predictable sensitivity allows an optimization process to adjust \(w\) gradually.
A binary selector
\[
I\in\{0,1\}
\]
cannot be changed by an arbitrarily small amount while remaining binary. It must jump from one admissible value to the other.
A continuous weight permits local adjustments:
\[
0.40
\longrightarrow
0.41
\longrightarrow
0.42.
\]
This does not by itself explain how learning occurs, but it establishes why soft gates are compatible with gradient-based adjustment. Their outputs vary continuously with their parameters.
The mathematical transition is
\[
\boxed{
\text{discrete choice}
\rightarrow
\text{continuous influence}
\rightarrow
\text{adjustable contribution}.
}
\]
This will become important when weights are produced or learned by machine-learning models.


The Complete Meaning-First Procedure
When encountering
\[
C=wA+(1-w)B,
\]
the reader should not immediately label it interpolation, probability, expectation, or attention.
Instead, ask:

What do \(A\) and \(B\) represent?
Do they belong to a space in which addition is meaningful?
What does multiplication by \(w\) mean?
What complete quantity is divided into the shares \(w\) and \(1-w\)?
Is \(C\) an actual state, a mixture property, a temporal average, an expected value, or a prediction?
Is \(w\) fixed, observed, calculated, estimated, or learned?
Are intermediate outputs meaningful in the problem domain?

Only after these questions are answered should the algebra receive an application-specific name.
The safe reasoning order is
\[
\boxed{
\text{problem semantics}
\rightarrow
\text{meaning of endpoints}
\rightarrow
\text{meaning of weights}
\rightarrow
\text{weighted equation}
\rightarrow
\text{interpretation of output}.
}
\]


The Completed Structure of Soft Selection
This chapter began with binary selection:
\[
I\in\{0,1\}.
\]
A hard selector chooses one of two endpoints:
\[
IA+(1-I)B.
\]
The selector domain was expanded to
\[
w\in[0,1],
\]
allowing partial influence.
Complementary shares produced the convex combination
\[
wA+(1-w)B.
\]
Algebraic rearrangement revealed the displacement form
\[
B+w(A-B).
\]
For weights in \([0,1]\), the expression interpolates between the endpoints. For weights outside that interval, it extrapolates along the same affine line.
Finally, the same equation was shown to support several distinct interpretations. The algebraic skeleton remains stable:
\[
\boxed{
C=wA+(1-w)B.
}
\]
The semantic model determines whether \(C\) is an intermediate state, physical mixture, time average, expectation, combined prediction, or softly gated output.
The chapter’s final principle is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\text{the equation determines how contributions combine;
the problem determines what those contributions mean}.
}
\]
Soft selection has introduced two complementary weights. The next chapter will generalize this structure from two alternatives to many:
\[
w_1A_1+w_2A_2+\cdots+w_nA_n.
\]
That generalization will require us to determine what conditions the weights must satisfy, why normalization matters, and how weighted combinations connect expectations, mixtures, model ensembles, and attention.

title: Chapter 13 — From Scores to Shares
text:
Chapter 12 studied computations of the form
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i,
\]
where each \(A_i\) is an alternative and each \(w_i\) determines how strongly that alternative contributes to the result. When the weights satisfy
\[
w_i\geq 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1,
\]
they divide one unit of total contribution among the alternatives. This interpretation gives the weights a specific mathematical role. They are not merely numbers placed beside the alternatives. They are shares of a conserved whole. Suppose three alternatives receive the weights
\[
\mathbf{w}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The first alternative receives \(20\%\) of the total influence, the second receives \(50\%\), and the third receives \(30\%\). Since
\[
0.2+0.5+0.3=1,
\]
the complete unit of influence has been allocated. A computational system, however, rarely begins by directly producing these shares. It commonly begins with numbers such as
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These numbers may indicate that the second alternative is supported more strongly than the third and that the third is supported more strongly than the first i.e \(s_2>s_3>s_1.\) They provide an ordering, but they do not yet explain how a total contribution should be divided. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
contains scores. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
contains shares. Their numerical resemblance should not conceal their different mathematical roles.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Scores compare alternatives; weights allocate contribution among alternatives.}
}
\]


Suppose a system must evaluate three possible explanations for an observation. After examining the input, it assigns the scores
\[
s_1=2,\qquad s_2=5,\qquad s_3=3.
\]
The score \(5\) indicates stronger support than the score \(3\), while the score \(3\) indicates stronger support than the score \(2\). The scores therefore provide a ranking:
\[
A_2 \succ A_3 \succ A_1.
\]
The symbol \(\succ\) means “is preferred to” or “receives stronger support than.” This ranking is meaningful even before we decide what proportion of influence each alternative should receive. If the task requires a hard choice, the system can select the largest score:
\[
k=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i}s_i.
\]
For the present scores,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i}s_i=2,
\]
so the selected alternative is \(A_2\). This operation uses the scores comparatively. It asks which position contains the largest value. It does not require the scores to be probabilities or normalized weights. In Python, the hard selection can be implemented as follows:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 3.0])

selected_index = np.argmax(scores)

print(selected_index)
The output is
1
because Python uses zero-based indexing. Index 1 corresponds to the second mathematical position, whose score is \(5\). If the alternatives are stored explicitly, the selected alternative can be recovered from the same index:
alternatives = np.array([20.0, 50.0, 80.0])

selected_index = np.argmax(scores)
selected_alternative = alternatives[selected_index]

print(selected_alternative)
The result is
50.0
The score vector has performed hard selection. Only the ordering matters. If the task instead requires a graded combination, the system must answer a different question. It must determine not merely which alternative is strongest, but how the total influence should be distributed:
\[
C=w_1A_1+w_2A_2+w_3A_3.
\]
The ranking
\[
s_2>s_3>s_1
\]
suggests that a reasonable transformation should produce
\[
w_2>w_3>w_1.
\]
But the ranking alone does not determine the numerical weights uniquely. All of the following weight vectors preserve the same ordering:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
0.05\\
0.80\\
0.15
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
0.30\\
0.36\\
0.34
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Each vector assigns the greatest weight to the second alternative, the next greatest weight to the third, and the smallest weight to the first. Nevertheless, they describe very different allocations. The first allocation moderately favors \(A_2\). The second strongly concentrates the contribution on \(A_2\). The third distributes the contribution almost evenly. Therefore, a score-to-weight transformation must determine more than order. It must also determine how score differences control the concentration of the resulting shares.



Consider alternatives
\[
A_1=20,\qquad A_2=50,\qquad A_3=80
\]
and scores
\[
s_1=2,\qquad s_2=5,\qquad s_3=3.
\]
If the scores are inserted directly into a weighted sum, the result is
\[
2(20)+5(50)+3(80)
=
40+250+240
=
530.
\]
This calculation is mathematically valid as a weighted sum:
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{3}s_iA_i.
\]
But it is not a weighted average because
\[
2+5+3=10\neq 1.
\]
The coefficients allocate ten units of total contribution rather than one. Consequently, the result is not constrained to remain between the smallest and largest alternatives:
\[
20\leq C\leq 80.
\]
Indeed,
\[
530>80.
\]
Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. The problem is interpretive. The numbers \(2\), \(5\), and \(3\) have been used as though they were shares even though they do not satisfy the structure required of shares. This distinction resembles the difference between an amount and a proportion. Suppose three containers contain
\[
2,\qquad 5,\qquad 3
\]
litres of water. These amounts sum to
\[
2+5+3=10\text{ litres}.
\]
The first container holds \(2\) litres, but its share of the total water is
\[
\frac{2}{10}=0.2.
\]
Similarly, the second and third shares are
\[
\frac{5}{10}=0.5
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{3}{10}=0.3.
\]
The amounts and the shares contain related information, but they are not the same objects:
\[
\boxed{
\text{share of an amount}
=
\frac{\text{individual amount}}{\text{total amount}}.
}
\]
The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
describes how much is present in each position. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
describes how the whole is divided among those positions. This suggests division by a total, which will be developed carefully in Section 13.2. Before adopting that construction, however, we must understand why arbitrary scores create additional difficulties.



Many computational scoring mechanisms produce negative values. A linear model, for example, may calculate a score from an input vector \(\mathbf{x}\) using
\[
s_i=\mathbf{a}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}+b_i.
\]
Because dot products and biases can produce any real number, the result may be
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-2\\
1\\
3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These scores remain meaningful as comparative assessments:
\[
3>1>-2.
\]
The third alternative receives the strongest support, while the first receives the weakest. But the negative score cannot directly represent a nonnegative share. If we attempted to use the scores as mixture proportions, we would obtain
\[
-2A_1+1A_2+3A_3.
\]
The coefficient \(-2\) would mean that the first alternative contributes negative two units of the mixture. Such coefficients may be perfectly meaningful in a general linear combination, where subtraction is allowed, but they do not describe an ordinary allocation of a positive whole. This reveals a hierarchy of mathematical structures:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{linear combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i a_iA_i,
&&a_i\in\mathbb{R},\\[4pt]
\text{affine combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i a_iA_i,
&&\sum_i a_i=1,\\[4pt]
\text{convex combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i w_iA_i,
&&w_i\geq 0,\quad \sum_iw_i=1.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Every convex combination is an affine combination, and every affine combination is a linear combination. The reverse implications do not generally hold. Scores may serve as coefficients in a linear combination, but this does not make them valid coefficients for a convex combination. To become shares, they must satisfy the stronger convex conditions.



It might appear that the only problem is the total. If the coefficients sum to one, perhaps they can always be interpreted as shares. Consider
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
-1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The entries satisfy
\[
2+(-1)+0=1.
\]
Yet the vector does not represent an ordinary division of one whole because one component is negative and another exceeds the whole:
\[
s_2=-1<0,
\qquad
s_1=2>1.
\]
The equation
\[
2A_1-A_2
\]
is an affine combination, but not a convex combination. For a finite collection of weights, the two essential conditions are therefore
\[
\sum_iw_i=1
\]
and
\[
w_i\geq 0
\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Together, these conditions also imply
\[
0\leq w_i\leq 1.
\]
To see why, suppose some weight \(w_k\) exceeded one. Since all the other weights are nonnegative,
\[
\sum_iw_i
\geq w_k
>1,
\]
which would contradict
\[
\sum_iw_i=1.
\]
Thus, the upper bound does not need to be imposed separately. Nonnegativity and a unit total already guarantee it.



Suppose a scoring system produces
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Numerically, this vector is already nonnegative and sums to one. It therefore belongs to the simplex and can mathematically serve as a weight vector. But its numerical form does not by itself prove that the system intended its values to be probabilities or shares. A score is defined not only by its current values but also by the process that produced it and the role it plays in the model. The next input might produce
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1.7\\
-0.4\\
2.1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If the scoring mechanism has no rule guaranteeing nonnegativity and a unit total, then its outputs are not generally normalized weights. The first output merely happened to satisfy the constraints.
This is the same distinction that appears throughout mathematical modeling: observing that an object possesses a property in one example is different from constructing a mechanism that guarantees the property in every permitted case. A proper score-to-weight transformation must provide a guarantee:
\[
\boxed{
\text{For every permitted score vector, the output must be a valid weight vector.}
}
\]



An unrestricted score vector has the form
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
(s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n)
\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Every coordinate may independently take any real value. Geometrically, the vector may occupy any point in \(n\)-dimensional real space. A valid weight vector belongs to the simplex
\[
\Delta^{n-1}
=
\left\{
\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
w_i\geq 0,\;
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1
\right\}.
\]
For three alternatives, the score vector belongs to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), while the weight vector belongs to
\[
\Delta^2
=
\left\{
(w_1,w_2,w_3):
w_i\geq 0,\;
w_1+w_2+w_3=1
\right\}.
\]
Although the weight vector has three coordinates, only two coordinates can be chosen independently. Once \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are known, the third is determined:
\[
w_3=1-w_1-w_2.
\]
The unit-sum condition removes one degree of freedom. This is why the set is denoted by \(\Delta^2\) rather than \(\Delta^3\). A normalization mechanism is therefore a function
\[
N:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
It receives an unrestricted vector and returns a constrained vector:
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
This transformation does not merely rescale isolated numbers. It creates a relationship among all positions. The weight assigned to one alternative depends not only on its own score but also on the scores assigned to the competing alternatives. This dependence is unavoidable because every weight is a share of a common total.



Suppose the first alternative has score
\[
s_1=2.
\]
Can we determine its weight from this number alone? The answer is no. Consider two score vectors:
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(a)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
1\\
1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{s}^{(b)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
10\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The first score is \(2\) in both vectors. Nevertheless, its relative position has changed. In the first vector, the score \(2\) is the largest:
\[
2>1.
\]
In the second vector, it is the smallest:
\[
2<10.
\]
A sensible allocation mechanism should not assign the same weight to the first alternative in both cases merely because its individual score remained \(2\). Its contribution must be interpreted relative to the entire collection. This is the defining nature of a share. A share does not describe an isolated amount; it describes an amount in relation to a whole. If
\[
w_i=\frac{a_i}{\sum_ja_j},
\]
then changing some other amount \(a_k\) changes the denominator and therefore changes \(w_i\), even when \(a_i\) remains fixed. The alternatives are coupled through the shared total.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Normalization turns independently stated strengths into mutually dependent shares.}
}
\]
Increasing the share of one alternative must be balanced by decreases elsewhere because the total remains fixed:
\[
\sum_iw_i=1.
\]
If the weights change from \(\mathbf{w}\) to \(\mathbf{w}+\Delta\mathbf{w}\), then
\[
\sum_i(w_i+\Delta w_i)=1.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_iw_i=1,
\]
it follows that
\[
\sum_i\Delta w_i=0.
\]
The total change across all weights must be zero. Weight cannot be created in one position without being removed, directly or indirectly, from other positions.



Given scores
\[
s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n,
\]
hard selection asks
\[
k=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i.
\]
The result is an index. It identifies the winning alternative. This decision can be represented by a one-hot vector:
\[
I_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=k,\\
0, & i\neq k.
\end{cases}
\]
The selected result is then
\[
C_{\text{hard}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}I_iA_i
=
A_k.
\]
Soft allocation instead constructs graded weights:
\[
w_i\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_iw_i=1,
\]
and produces
\[
C_{\text{soft}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i.
\]
Hard selection preserves only the identity of the largest score. It discards the sizes of the differences among the scores. For example, consider
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(a)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
5.0\\
4.9\\
1.0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(b)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
50\\
1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
In both cases,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i=1.
\]
Hard selection treats both vectors identically: the first alternative wins. But the relationships among the scores are very different. In the first vector, the first and second alternatives are nearly tied:
\[
5.0-4.9=0.1.
\]
In the second vector, the first alternative dominates the second:
\[
50-1=49.
\]
A soft transformation can preserve information about these differences by producing a diffuse allocation for the near tie and a concentrated allocation for the decisive separation. This is one reason soft weighting is useful in machine learning. It allows the system to express degrees of comparative support rather than immediately collapsing every competition into a single winner.



We can now derive the basic requirements of a transformation
\[
N:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
Let
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The first requirement is nonnegativity:
\[
w_i\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
Without this condition, the output cannot represent ordinary shares, probabilities, mixture proportions, or nonnegative contribution strengths. The second requirement is unit total:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1.
\]
This converts the collection into an allocation of one whole. The third requirement is order preservation. If one score is larger than another,
\[
s_i>s_j,
\]
then the resulting weight should ordinarily satisfy
\[
w_i>w_j.
\]
A transformation that assigned less weight to the more strongly supported alternative would reverse the meaning of the score ordering. The fourth requirement is equal treatment of equal scores. If
\[
s_i=s_j,
\]
then there is no score-based reason to favor one of the two positions. We therefore expect
\[
w_i=w_j.
\]
More generally, if all scores are equal,
\[
s_1=s_2=\cdots=s_n,
\]
symmetry requires uniform weights:
\[
w_1=w_2=\cdots=w_n=\frac{1}{n}.
\]
The fifth requirement is continuity. A small change in the scores should usually produce a small change in the weights. If tiny measurement noise caused the allocation to jump abruptly from one extreme to another, the transformation would behave like hard selection rather than soft allocation. Symbolically, if
\[
\mathbf{s}'\approx\mathbf{s},
\]
then we want
\[
N(\mathbf{s}')\approx N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The sixth requirement is permutation consistency. The numerical position of an alternative should not give it special treatment. If we reorder the scores, apply the transformation, and then restore the original order, we should recover the same corresponding weights.
If \(P\) is a permutation matrix, this requirement can be written as
\[
N(P\mathbf{s})=PN(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The transformation follows the alternatives when they are reordered. A further desirable property is that the weights depend on relative evidence rather than on an arbitrary shared baseline. If the same constant \(c\) is added to every score, the comparisons remain unchanged:
\[
(s_i+c)-(s_j+c)=s_i-s_j.
\]
This suggests the invariance
\[
N(\mathbf{s}+c\mathbf{1})=N(\mathbf{s}),
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
\vdots\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Softmax will satisfy this property exactly. Its significance will become clearer when we derive the transformation in later sections. The desired behavior can be summarized as follows:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^n
\quad\longmapsto\quad
\mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{n-1}
\end{aligned}
}
\]
such that the output is nonnegative, sums to one, respects score ordering, treats equal scores equally, changes smoothly, and does not depend on the arbitrary ordering of the alternatives.



In a multiclass machine-learning model, the final layer may produce one score for each possible class:
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1\\
s_2\\
\vdots\\
s_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These raw class scores are often called logits. A logit is not automatically a probability. It is an unrestricted real number produced before the final normalization step. For example, an image classifier might produce
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1.2\\
2.4\\
0.7
\end{bmatrix}
\]
for the classes
\[
\text{cat},\qquad
\text{dog},\qquad
\text{bird}.
\]
The ordering
\[
2.4>0.7>-1.2
\]
shows that the model currently gives the strongest support to dog, followed by bird, and then cat. The prediction can be obtained through
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i,
\]
but the scores themselves should not be displayed as class probabilities:
\[
-1.2,\qquad 2.4,\qquad 0.7.
\]
A negative probability would be invalid, and a probability greater than one would also be invalid. Furthermore,
\[
-1.2+2.4+0.7=1.9\neq 1.
\]
The scores must first be transformed into a point on the simplex. This distinction prevents a common conceptual error:
\[
\boxed{
\text{A model score measures comparative support; it is not yet a probability assigned to an event.}
}
\]
After a normalization such as softmax, the output may have the mathematical form of a probability distribution. Even then, interpreting it as a trustworthy estimate of real-world uncertainty requires further assumptions and empirical calibration. Normalization guarantees mathematical validity; it does not by itself guarantee that the model’s confidence corresponds to reality.



The complete problem can now be stated. We begin with unrestricted scores:
\[
\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
These scores may be positive, zero, or negative. They may have any total. Their primary role is to express relative support among alternatives. We require a transformation that produces
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}),
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
The resulting weights can then participate in the weighted combination
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i.
\]
The computational journey is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\text{alternatives}
\longrightarrow
\text{comparative scores}
\longrightarrow
\text{normalized shares}
\longrightarrow
\text{weighted result}.
}
\]
The first arrow evaluates the alternatives. The second converts unrestricted evaluations into a valid allocation. The third uses that allocation to construct an output. Chapter 12 studied the final arrow. The present chapter studies the middle arrow. The most immediate way to construct a share is to divide an individual amount by a total amount:
\[
\text{share}
=
\frac{\text{individual amount}}
{\text{total amount}}.
\]
Applied to a collection of nonnegative quantities, this suggests
\[
w_i
=
\frac{s_i}{\sum_js_j}.
\]
This formula appears simple, but its simplicity hides several assumptions. What happens if the total is zero? What happens if some scores are negative? What happens if positive and negative scores cancel one another? Which properties does division preserve, and which problems does it fail to solve? These questions lead to ordinary normalization, the subject of the next section.

title: Chapter 13 — From Scores to Shares
text:
Chapter 12 studied computations of the form
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i,
\]
where each \(A_i\) is an alternative and each \(w_i\) determines how strongly that alternative contributes to the result. When the weights satisfy
\[
w_i\geq 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1,
\]
they divide one unit of total contribution among the alternatives. This interpretation gives the weights a specific mathematical role. They are not merely numbers placed beside the alternatives. They are shares of a conserved whole. Suppose three alternatives receive the weights
\[
\mathbf{w}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The first alternative receives \(20\%\) of the total influence, the second receives \(50\%\), and the third receives \(30\%\). Since
\[
0.2+0.5+0.3=1,
\]
the complete unit of influence has been allocated. A computational system, however, rarely begins by directly producing these shares. It commonly begins with numbers such as
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These numbers may indicate that the second alternative is supported more strongly than the third and that the third is supported more strongly than the first i.e \(s_2>s_3>s_1.\) They provide an ordering, but they do not yet explain how a total contribution should be divided. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
contains scores. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
contains shares. Their numerical resemblance should not conceal their different mathematical roles.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Scores compare alternatives; weights allocate contribution among alternatives.}
}
\]


Suppose a system must evaluate three possible explanations for an observation. After examining the input, it assigns the scores
\[
s_1=2,\qquad s_2=5,\qquad s_3=3.
\]
The score \(5\) indicates stronger support than the score \(3\), while the score \(3\) indicates stronger support than the score \(2\). The scores therefore provide a ranking:
\[
A_2 \succ A_3 \succ A_1.
\]
The symbol \(\succ\) means “is preferred to” or “receives stronger support than.” This ranking is meaningful even before we decide what proportion of influence each alternative should receive. If the task requires a hard choice, the system can select the largest score:
\[
k=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i}s_i.
\]
For the present scores,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i}s_i=2,
\]
so the selected alternative is \(A_2\). This operation uses the scores comparatively. It asks which position contains the largest value. It does not require the scores to be probabilities or normalized weights. In Python, the hard selection can be implemented as follows:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([2.0, 5.0, 3.0])

selected_index = np.argmax(scores)

print(selected_index)
The output is
1
because Python uses zero-based indexing. Index 1 corresponds to the second mathematical position, whose score is \(5\). If the alternatives are stored explicitly, the selected alternative can be recovered from the same index:
alternatives = np.array([20.0, 50.0, 80.0])

selected_index = np.argmax(scores)
selected_alternative = alternatives[selected_index]

print(selected_alternative)
The result is
50.0
The score vector has performed hard selection. Only the ordering matters. If the task instead requires a graded combination, the system must answer a different question. It must determine not merely which alternative is strongest, but how the total influence should be distributed:
\[
C=w_1A_1+w_2A_2+w_3A_3.
\]
The ranking
\[
s_2>s_3>s_1
\]
suggests that a reasonable transformation should produce
\[
w_2>w_3>w_1.
\]
But the ranking alone does not determine the numerical weights uniquely. All of the following weight vectors preserve the same ordering:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
0.05\\
0.80\\
0.15
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
0.30\\
0.36\\
0.34
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Each vector assigns the greatest weight to the second alternative, the next greatest weight to the third, and the smallest weight to the first. Nevertheless, they describe very different allocations. The first allocation moderately favors \(A_2\). The second strongly concentrates the contribution on \(A_2\). The third distributes the contribution almost evenly. Therefore, a score-to-weight transformation must determine more than order. It must also determine how score differences control the concentration of the resulting shares.



Consider alternatives
\[
A_1=20,\qquad A_2=50,\qquad A_3=80
\]
and scores
\[
s_1=2,\qquad s_2=5,\qquad s_3=3.
\]
If the scores are inserted directly into a weighted sum, the result is
\[
2(20)+5(50)+3(80)
=
40+250+240
=
530.
\]
This calculation is mathematically valid as a weighted sum:
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{3}s_iA_i.
\]
But it is not a weighted average because
\[
2+5+3=10\neq 1.
\]
The coefficients allocate ten units of total contribution rather than one. Consequently, the result is not constrained to remain between the smallest and largest alternatives:
\[
20\leq C\leq 80.
\]
Indeed,
\[
530>80.
\]
Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. The problem is interpretive. The numbers \(2\), \(5\), and \(3\) have been used as though they were shares even though they do not satisfy the structure required of shares. This distinction resembles the difference between an amount and a proportion. Suppose three containers contain
\[
2,\qquad 5,\qquad 3
\]
litres of water. These amounts sum to
\[
2+5+3=10\text{ litres}.
\]
The first container holds \(2\) litres, but its share of the total water is
\[
\frac{2}{10}=0.2.
\]
Similarly, the second and third shares are
\[
\frac{5}{10}=0.5
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{3}{10}=0.3.
\]
The amounts and the shares contain related information, but they are not the same objects:
\[
\boxed{
\text{share of an amount}
=
\frac{\text{individual amount}}{\text{total amount}}.
}
\]
The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
describes how much is present in each position. The vector
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}
\]
describes how the whole is divided among those positions. This suggests division by a total, which will be developed carefully in Section 13.2. Before adopting that construction, however, we must understand why arbitrary scores create additional difficulties.



Many computational scoring mechanisms produce negative values. A linear model, for example, may calculate a score from an input vector \(\mathbf{x}\) using
\[
s_i=\mathbf{a}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}+b_i.
\]
Because dot products and biases can produce any real number, the result may be
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-2\\
1\\
3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These scores remain meaningful as comparative assessments:
\[
3>1>-2.
\]
The third alternative receives the strongest support, while the first receives the weakest. But the negative score cannot directly represent a nonnegative share. If we attempted to use the scores as mixture proportions, we would obtain
\[
-2A_1+1A_2+3A_3.
\]
The coefficient \(-2\) would mean that the first alternative contributes negative two units of the mixture. Such coefficients may be perfectly meaningful in a general linear combination, where subtraction is allowed, but they do not describe an ordinary allocation of a positive whole. This reveals a hierarchy of mathematical structures:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{linear combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i a_iA_i,
&&a_i\in\mathbb{R},\\[4pt]
\text{affine combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i a_iA_i,
&&\sum_i a_i=1,\\[4pt]
\text{convex combination:}\quad
&C=\sum_i w_iA_i,
&&w_i\geq 0,\quad \sum_iw_i=1.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
Every convex combination is an affine combination, and every affine combination is a linear combination. The reverse implications do not generally hold. Scores may serve as coefficients in a linear combination, but this does not make them valid coefficients for a convex combination. To become shares, they must satisfy the stronger convex conditions.



It might appear that the only problem is the total. If the coefficients sum to one, perhaps they can always be interpreted as shares. Consider
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
-1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The entries satisfy
\[
2+(-1)+0=1.
\]
Yet the vector does not represent an ordinary division of one whole because one component is negative and another exceeds the whole:
\[
s_2=-1<0,
\qquad
s_1=2>1.
\]
The equation
\[
2A_1-A_2
\]
is an affine combination, but not a convex combination. For a finite collection of weights, the two essential conditions are therefore
\[
\sum_iw_i=1
\]
and
\[
w_i\geq 0
\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Together, these conditions also imply
\[
0\leq w_i\leq 1.
\]
To see why, suppose some weight \(w_k\) exceeded one. Since all the other weights are nonnegative,
\[
\sum_iw_i
\geq w_k
>1,
\]
which would contradict
\[
\sum_iw_i=1.
\]
Thus, the upper bound does not need to be imposed separately. Nonnegativity and a unit total already guarantee it.



Suppose a scoring system produces
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Numerically, this vector is already nonnegative and sums to one. It therefore belongs to the simplex and can mathematically serve as a weight vector. But its numerical form does not by itself prove that the system intended its values to be probabilities or shares. A score is defined not only by its current values but also by the process that produced it and the role it plays in the model. The next input might produce
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1.7\\
-0.4\\
2.1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If the scoring mechanism has no rule guaranteeing nonnegativity and a unit total, then its outputs are not generally normalized weights. The first output merely happened to satisfy the constraints.
This is the same distinction that appears throughout mathematical modeling: observing that an object possesses a property in one example is different from constructing a mechanism that guarantees the property in every permitted case. A proper score-to-weight transformation must provide a guarantee:
\[
\boxed{
\text{For every permitted score vector, the output must be a valid weight vector.}
}
\]



An unrestricted score vector has the form
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
(s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n)
\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Every coordinate may independently take any real value. Geometrically, the vector may occupy any point in \(n\)-dimensional real space. A valid weight vector belongs to the simplex
\[
\Delta^{n-1}
=
\left\{
\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^n:
w_i\geq 0,\;
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1
\right\}.
\]
For three alternatives, the score vector belongs to \(\mathbb{R}^3\), while the weight vector belongs to
\[
\Delta^2
=
\left\{
(w_1,w_2,w_3):
w_i\geq 0,\;
w_1+w_2+w_3=1
\right\}.
\]
Although the weight vector has three coordinates, only two coordinates can be chosen independently. Once \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) are known, the third is determined:
\[
w_3=1-w_1-w_2.
\]
The unit-sum condition removes one degree of freedom. This is why the set is denoted by \(\Delta^2\) rather than \(\Delta^3\). A normalization mechanism is therefore a function
\[
N:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
It receives an unrestricted vector and returns a constrained vector:
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
This transformation does not merely rescale isolated numbers. It creates a relationship among all positions. The weight assigned to one alternative depends not only on its own score but also on the scores assigned to the competing alternatives. This dependence is unavoidable because every weight is a share of a common total.



Suppose the first alternative has score
\[
s_1=2.
\]
Can we determine its weight from this number alone? The answer is no. Consider two score vectors:
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(a)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
1\\
1
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{s}^{(b)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
10\\
10
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The first score is \(2\) in both vectors. Nevertheless, its relative position has changed. In the first vector, the score \(2\) is the largest:
\[
2>1.
\]
In the second vector, it is the smallest:
\[
2<10.
\]
A sensible allocation mechanism should not assign the same weight to the first alternative in both cases merely because its individual score remained \(2\). Its contribution must be interpreted relative to the entire collection. This is the defining nature of a share. A share does not describe an isolated amount; it describes an amount in relation to a whole. If
\[
w_i=\frac{a_i}{\sum_ja_j},
\]
then changing some other amount \(a_k\) changes the denominator and therefore changes \(w_i\), even when \(a_i\) remains fixed. The alternatives are coupled through the shared total.
\[
\boxed{
\text{Normalization turns independently stated strengths into mutually dependent shares.}
}
\]
Increasing the share of one alternative must be balanced by decreases elsewhere because the total remains fixed:
\[
\sum_iw_i=1.
\]
If the weights change from \(\mathbf{w}\) to \(\mathbf{w}+\Delta\mathbf{w}\), then
\[
\sum_i(w_i+\Delta w_i)=1.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_iw_i=1,
\]
it follows that
\[
\sum_i\Delta w_i=0.
\]
The total change across all weights must be zero. Weight cannot be created in one position without being removed, directly or indirectly, from other positions.



Given scores
\[
s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n,
\]
hard selection asks
\[
k=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i.
\]
The result is an index. It identifies the winning alternative. This decision can be represented by a one-hot vector:
\[
I_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=k,\\
0, & i\neq k.
\end{cases}
\]
The selected result is then
\[
C_{\text{hard}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}I_iA_i
=
A_k.
\]
Soft allocation instead constructs graded weights:
\[
w_i\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_iw_i=1,
\]
and produces
\[
C_{\text{soft}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i.
\]
Hard selection preserves only the identity of the largest score. It discards the sizes of the differences among the scores. For example, consider
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(a)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
5.0\\
4.9\\
1.0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\mathbf{s}^{(b)}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
50\\
1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
In both cases,
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i=1.
\]
Hard selection treats both vectors identically: the first alternative wins. But the relationships among the scores are very different. In the first vector, the first and second alternatives are nearly tied:
\[
5.0-4.9=0.1.
\]
In the second vector, the first alternative dominates the second:
\[
50-1=49.
\]
A soft transformation can preserve information about these differences by producing a diffuse allocation for the near tie and a concentrated allocation for the decisive separation. This is one reason soft weighting is useful in machine learning. It allows the system to express degrees of comparative support rather than immediately collapsing every competition into a single winner.



We can now derive the basic requirements of a transformation
\[
N:\mathbb{R}^n\longrightarrow\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
Let
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The first requirement is nonnegativity:
\[
w_i\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
Without this condition, the output cannot represent ordinary shares, probabilities, mixture proportions, or nonnegative contribution strengths. The second requirement is unit total:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i=1.
\]
This converts the collection into an allocation of one whole. The third requirement is order preservation. If one score is larger than another,
\[
s_i>s_j,
\]
then the resulting weight should ordinarily satisfy
\[
w_i>w_j.
\]
A transformation that assigned less weight to the more strongly supported alternative would reverse the meaning of the score ordering. The fourth requirement is equal treatment of equal scores. If
\[
s_i=s_j,
\]
then there is no score-based reason to favor one of the two positions. We therefore expect
\[
w_i=w_j.
\]
More generally, if all scores are equal,
\[
s_1=s_2=\cdots=s_n,
\]
symmetry requires uniform weights:
\[
w_1=w_2=\cdots=w_n=\frac{1}{n}.
\]
The fifth requirement is continuity. A small change in the scores should usually produce a small change in the weights. If tiny measurement noise caused the allocation to jump abruptly from one extreme to another, the transformation would behave like hard selection rather than soft allocation. Symbolically, if
\[
\mathbf{s}'\approx\mathbf{s},
\]
then we want
\[
N(\mathbf{s}')\approx N(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The sixth requirement is permutation consistency. The numerical position of an alternative should not give it special treatment. If we reorder the scores, apply the transformation, and then restore the original order, we should recover the same corresponding weights.
If \(P\) is a permutation matrix, this requirement can be written as
\[
N(P\mathbf{s})=PN(\mathbf{s}).
\]
The transformation follows the alternatives when they are reordered. A further desirable property is that the weights depend on relative evidence rather than on an arbitrary shared baseline. If the same constant \(c\) is added to every score, the comparisons remain unchanged:
\[
(s_i+c)-(s_j+c)=s_i-s_j.
\]
This suggests the invariance
\[
N(\mathbf{s}+c\mathbf{1})=N(\mathbf{s}),
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
\vdots\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Softmax will satisfy this property exactly. Its significance will become clearer when we derive the transformation in later sections. The desired behavior can be summarized as follows:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^n
\quad\longmapsto\quad
\mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{n-1}
\end{aligned}
}
\]
such that the output is nonnegative, sums to one, respects score ordering, treats equal scores equally, changes smoothly, and does not depend on the arbitrary ordering of the alternatives.



In a multiclass machine-learning model, the final layer may produce one score for each possible class:
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
s_1\\
s_2\\
\vdots\\
s_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
These raw class scores are often called logits. A logit is not automatically a probability. It is an unrestricted real number produced before the final normalization step. For example, an image classifier might produce
\[
\mathbf{s}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1.2\\
2.4\\
0.7
\end{bmatrix}
\]
for the classes
\[
\text{cat},\qquad
\text{dog},\qquad
\text{bird}.
\]
The ordering
\[
2.4>0.7>-1.2
\]
shows that the model currently gives the strongest support to dog, followed by bird, and then cat. The prediction can be obtained through
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i s_i,
\]
but the scores themselves should not be displayed as class probabilities:
\[
-1.2,\qquad 2.4,\qquad 0.7.
\]
A negative probability would be invalid, and a probability greater than one would also be invalid. Furthermore,
\[
-1.2+2.4+0.7=1.9\neq 1.
\]
The scores must first be transformed into a point on the simplex. This distinction prevents a common conceptual error:
\[
\boxed{
\text{A model score measures comparative support; it is not yet a probability assigned to an event.}
}
\]
After a normalization such as softmax, the output may have the mathematical form of a probability distribution. Even then, interpreting it as a trustworthy estimate of real-world uncertainty requires further assumptions and empirical calibration. Normalization guarantees mathematical validity; it does not by itself guarantee that the model’s confidence corresponds to reality.



The complete problem can now be stated. We begin with unrestricted scores:
\[
\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
These scores may be positive, zero, or negative. They may have any total. Their primary role is to express relative support among alternatives. We require a transformation that produces
\[
\mathbf{w}=N(\mathbf{s}),
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{n-1}.
\]
The resulting weights can then participate in the weighted combination
\[
C=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iA_i.
\]
The computational journey is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\text{alternatives}
\longrightarrow
\text{comparative scores}
\longrightarrow
\text{normalized shares}
\longrightarrow
\text{weighted result}.
}
\]
The first arrow evaluates the alternatives. The second converts unrestricted evaluations into a valid allocation. The third uses that allocation to construct an output. Chapter 12 studied the final arrow. The present chapter studies the middle arrow. The most immediate way to construct a share is to divide an individual amount by a total amount:
\[
\text{share}
=
\frac{\text{individual amount}}
{\text{total amount}}.
\]
Applied to a collection of nonnegative quantities, this suggests
\[
w_i
=
\frac{s_i}{\sum_js_j}.
\]
This formula appears simple, but its simplicity hides several assumptions. What happens if the total is zero? What happens if some scores are negative? What happens if positive and negative scores cancel one another? Which properties does division preserve, and which problems does it fail to solve? These questions lead to ordinary normalization, the subject of the next section.

title: Chapter 13 — From Scores to Shares
section: 13.2 Normalization as Division by a Total
text:
13.2 Normalization as Division by a Total
Section 13.1 established that a score and a share are different mathematical objects. A score expresses the strength assigned to an alternative, while a share expresses that alternative’s contribution relative to a whole. If the alternatives receive nonnegative amounts
\[
a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n,
\]
then their total amount is
\[
T=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j.
\]
Provided that
\[
T>0,
\]
the share belonging to alternative \(i\) is
\[
\boxed{
w_i=\frac{a_i}{T}
=
\frac{a_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j}.
}
\]
This equation is not an arbitrary mathematical convention. It follows directly from the meaning of a share. The numerator identifies the amount belonging to one alternative, while the denominator identifies the total amount across all alternatives. Division asks how much of the total is accounted for by the selected part:
\[
\boxed{
\text{share}
=
\frac{\text{part}}{\text{whole}}.
}
\]
Normalization by a total converts absolute amounts into relative amounts. The original values answer the question, “How much does each alternative possess?” The normalized values answer the question, “What fraction of everything belongs to each alternative?”

Constructing shares from amounts
Suppose three alternatives receive the positive strengths
\[
a_1=2,\qquad a_2=5,\qquad a_3=3.
\]
Their total strength is
\[
T=2+5+3=10.
\]
The normalized weights are therefore
\[
w_1=\frac{2}{10}=0.2,
\]
\[
w_2=\frac{5}{10}=0.5,
\]
and
\[
w_3=\frac{3}{10}=0.3.
\]
Thus,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
2\\
5\\
3
\end{bmatrix}
\longrightarrow
\begin{bmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The transformation has not changed which alternative is strongest. It has changed the numerical language in which the strengths are expressed. Before normalization, the second alternative has strength \(5\). After normalization, it possesses one-half of the total strength:
\[
\frac{5}{10}=0.5.
\]
Similarly, the first alternative possesses one-fifth of the total:
\[
\frac{2}{10}=0.2,
\]
while the third possesses three-tenths:
\[
\frac{3}{10}=0.3.
\]
The original values describe amounts measured against zero. The normalized values describe proportions measured against their collective total. In vector notation, let
\[
\mathbf{a}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a_1\\
a_2\\
\vdots\\
a_n
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If \(\mathbf{1}\) denotes the vector of ones,
\[
\mathbf{1}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
1\\
\vdots\\
1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
then the total is
\[
T=\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{a}.
\]
Normalization can therefore be written as
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf{w}
=
\frac{\mathbf{a}}
{\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{a}}.
}
\]
Division by the scalar total is applied to every coordinate of the vector.


Why the normalized values sum to one
The unit-sum property is not something that must be checked independently after normalization. It follows algebraically from the construction. Starting with
\[
w_i=\frac{a_i}{\sum_ja_j},
\]
we sum all normalized values:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{a_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j}.
\]
The denominator is the same for every term, so it can be placed beneath the sum of the numerators:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i}
{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j}.
\]
The letters \(i\) and \(j\) are merely indexing symbols. Both sums represent the same total. Therefore,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i
=
\frac{T}{T}
=
1,
\]
provided that
\[
T\neq 0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\sum_i
\frac{a_i}{\sum_ja_j}
=
1.
}
\]
The denominator does not merely make the values smaller. It makes their total equal to one because every numerator is being measured against the same complete total. This is a general pattern in mathematics:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\text{part}_1}{\text{whole}}
+
\frac{\text{part}_2}{\text{whole}}
+\cdots+
